category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How is 'Injury' legally defined in Forensic Medicine?
back: Any harm illegally caused to any person in body, mind, reputation, or property.
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury is any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the pathophysiological mechanism of a bruise (contusion)?
back: Sudden tissue indentation and recoil breaks blood vessels, causing extravasation of blood into surrounding tissue without breaking the skin surface.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil. ... Extravasations of blood from the broken vessels spread into the surrounding tissue.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Contrast the mechanism of split vs. over-stretch lacerations.
back: Split: Skin is crushed between weapon and underlying bone. Over-stretch: Localized pressure with push causes skin to flap and tear from underlying tissue.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page)-58: [Split laceration occurs ... where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. ... Over-stretch laceration ... pressure along with push causes breach of skin and its tear from the underlying tissue.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How does the 'architecture' of a body part determine wound type?
back: Tissues respond based on density/rigidity; a strike to the scalp (over bone) produces laceration, whereas a strike to the buttocks (soft tissue) produces a bruise.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike with a club ... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What biochemical step causes the green color in a healing bruise?
back: Tissue enzymes convert hemoglobin into blood pigments (biliverdin), typically occurring 4–5 days after injury.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What are the diagnostic criteria for an incised wound?
back: Linear/spindle shape, clean-cut margins, sharp angles, smooth walls, and absence of tissue bridging.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [It shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls. ... Wound is generally linear or spindle shaped.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of 'temporary cavitation' in firearm injuries.
back: High-velocity bullets dissipate kinetic energy radially, momentarily pushing soft tissues outward to create a cavity much larger than the bullet diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet ... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally ... creating instant cavitation.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Contrast Primary and Secondary effects of a bomb blast.
back: Primary: Direct impact of pressure wave front (>100 lb/sq inch) causing internal bruising. Secondary: Injuries from flying debris and fragments.
citation: Page 76 (Book Page)-77: [Primary effect is direct impact of steep pressure wave's front ... Secondary effect is an indirect consequence ... due to impact received by the victims due to debris.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the physiological loop causing death in domestic electrical contact?
back: 220-240V causes 'Hold-on effect' via muscle spasm, followed by ventricular fibrillation or respiratory center paralysis in the medulla.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): ['Hold-on effect' at 220-240V ... causes muscle spasm ... electrical contact causes long periods of apnea, ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the hallmark histological vital reaction in ante-mortem burns?
back: Leucocyte infiltration and increased enzyme activity (e.g., alkaline phosphatase) at the burn periphery.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration ... Histo-chemistry at the periphery of the burnt skin indicates increased enzymes reaction.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How is an injury defined from a medical perspective?
back: Any break in the body tissue, externally or internally. Medically, 'wound' and 'injury' are synonymous and represent a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of a 'split' or 'crush' laceration.
back: Sudden compression of skin and tissues between a blunt weapon and underlying bone splits the tissue. It occurs on sites like the scalp and may resemble an incised wound.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues betweenn the weapon and the underlying bone split them. It may resemble an incision wound.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Differentiate between ante-mortem and post-mortem abrasions.
back: Ante-mortem abrasions show vital reactions like redness or scabs. Post-mortem abrasions lack vital reactions and become dried, brown, and parchment-like with time.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying present appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the pathological significance of 'marbling' in a decomposing corpse?
back: Gases from putrefaction force blood into systemic veins. Bacteria (Clostridium Welchii) cause hemolysis, and liberated hemoglobin stains vessel walls, creating a visible linear pattern on the skin.
citation: Page 132 (Book Page): They invade the main systemic veins through the portal circulation and disrupt blood causing hemolysis and staining the tissues and the skin of the cadaver.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the pharmacological mechanism of Naloxone in opioid injury management?
back: It acts as a pure narcotic antagonist, competing with opioids at neuroreceptor sites to reverse respiratory depression, coma, and convulsions.
citation: Page 169 (Book Page): Naloxone is a pure narcotic antagonist and is the recommended drug of choice for reversal of overdose doses of narcotic analgesics, particularly in the presence of respiratory depression, coma and convulsions.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What are the five classical internal pathological hallmarks of fatal asphyxia?
back: 1. Generalized cyanosis. 2. Vascular congestion. 3. Tissue/visceral edema. 4. Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots). 5. Fluidity of blood.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): Table 13.1: General pathological changes in asphyxia • Generalized cyanosis • Vascular congestion • Edema of the tissues and viscera • Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera • Fluidity of blood

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Explain the 'cavitation' effect caused by high-velocity bullet injuries.
back: Energy radiates radially, creating a temporary cavity much larger than the bullet. Tissues recoil and collapse, leaving a permanent cavity of disorganized and shattered tissue.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... tissues recoil and collapse back leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How is 'pseudo-bruising' differentiated from a true ante-mortem bruise?
back: True bruises involve extravasated blood in tissues and show vital reactions (swelling). Pseudo-bruises are post-mortem hypostasis within vessels, lacking vital reaction or tissue infiltration.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Table 6.3: Bruise (Anti-mortem)... Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue... shows vital reaction (swelling and inflammation).

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the biochemical loop in organo-phosphorus poisoning.
back: Inhibition of acetyl-cholinesterase leads to acetylcholine accumulation. This causes excessive stimulation of muscarinic and nicotinic receptors, resulting in respiratory failure and cardiac arrest.
citation: Page 189 (Book Page): these compounds is that they inhibit the action of pseudo-cholinesterase in blood and acetyl-cholinesterase in red blood cells and at synaptic junctions. Thus, acetylcholine level increases, which binds to muscarinic and nicotinic receptors.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Which neck structures are most prone to fracture in manual throttling?
back: The greater cornua of the hyoid bone and the superior horns of the thyroid cartilage, particularly when calcified in older victims.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the defining medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: Any break in body tissue, occurring either externally in the skin or internally in serous membranes or organs. Both terms are synonymous pathological entities.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view. any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological mechanism of a 'Split Laceration.'
back: Sudden compression of skin/tissue between a blunt weapon and underlying bone causes the tissue to split. It may clinically resemble an incised wound.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split laceration occurs on scalp, forehead, chin or any other part of the body where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues betweenn the weapon and the underlying bone split them.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Contrast the margins of incised versus lacerated wounds.
back: Incised wounds: Clean-cut margins, sharp angles, and smooth walls. Lacerated wounds: Irregular margins, ill-defined angles, and bridging tissue tags.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page) (Table 6.4): [Incised: Clean cut margins, sharp angles, smooth walls. Lacerated: Irregular margins, ill defined angles, bridging tissue tags.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Explain the mechanism behind a 'Black Eye' occurring after a forehead strike.
back: Gravity Shifting: Effused blood from the original forehead injury moves along tissue lines of least resistance under gravitational influence into the lax periorbital area.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to dependent region under the influence of gravity within first few hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Which enzyme changes identify ante-mortem skin burns via histochemistry?
back: Increased reaction of alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, and non-specific esterase at the burn periphery. These appear earlier than traditional histological changes.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes... Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: List the four essential parts of a Firearm Wound-Complex.
back:
1. Entry wound
2. Trajectory with direction
3. Bullet resting place
4. Exit wound
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex is name allocated to some-total resultant damage findings of fire-blast on target. It has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Contrast low-velocity versus high-velocity bullet pathophysiology in soft tissue.
back: Low-velocity: Perforates tissue with damage proportionate to bullet diameter. High-velocity: Produces massive temporary cavitation and lateral tissue displacement, causing extensive disorganization.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Low velocity bullet while striking the body part... damage proportionate to diameter of the bullet... High velocity bullet, on the other hand, additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Differentiate 'contact' versus 'far-distance' shotgun entry wounds.
back: Contact: Single en-masse entry with burnt irregular margins. Far-distance: No central entry; widely dispersed pellets create individual holes without charring.
citation: Page 74 (Book Page): [Contact wound makes single en-my entry with burnt irregular margin... Far distance wound lacks central en-mass entry and pellets with wider dispersion make individual holes almost of the size of each pellet withoutt charing.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the mechanism of death in Traumatic Asphyxia?
back: Anoxic Anoxia: Caused by immobilization of the chest under heavy weight or crowd pressure, preventing expansion and respiratory movement.
citation: Page 155 (Book Page): [Traumatic asphyxia is immobilization of chest and is always accidental... Mechanism of death is anoxic anoxia.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Why is 'Cherry Red' discoloration observed in Carbon Monoxide poisoning?
back: CO has 200-300 times greater affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, forming stable carboxy-hemoglobin, which is bright cherry red in color.
citation: Page 187 (Book Page): [CO has 200-300 umes higher affinity for hemoglobin than Qs... It combines with hemoglobin to form carboxy-hemoglobin, which is cherry red in color.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the defining histological feature of an ante-mortem abrasion?
back: The presence of a vital reaction, including swelling and inflammation, which differentiates it from post-mortem marks.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the biochemical progression of color changes in a bruise.
back: Hemoglobin converts to pigments: Purple (fresh) -> Green (4-5 days) -> Yellow (7-10 days) -> Disappears.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How does blood location differ between a bruise and hypostasis (postmortem lividity)?
back: Bruise: Blood is extravasated into surrounding tissue spaces. Hypostasis: Blood remains within the vessels (intravascular).
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Bruise (anti-mortem): Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue... Post-mortem lividity: Blood is within the vessels and when incised, it flows from the mouths of the blood vessel.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Why do high-velocity bullets cause massive internal tissue destruction beyond their diameter?
back: Due to temporary cavitation; high kinetic energy dissipates radially, causing tissues to expand and collapse violently.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues... Energy in the bullet is very high and it tends to dissipate in the surrounding tissues more effectively in radial fashion creating instant cavitation.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the primary cause of cardiac death in low-voltage electrical injuries?
back: Ventricular fibrillation caused by direct action on the pacemaker and conducting system of the heart.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): [Low voltage produces myocardial fibrillation due to direct action on pace maker, conducting system and actual muscle fibers.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What macroscopic indicator confirms a thermal burn was sustained before death?
back: A line of redness (hyperemia) bordering the lesion and presence of albumin-rich plasma in blisters.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the mechanism of primary blast injury in air-filled organs?
back: Direct impact of steep pressure waves causing shearing movements, bruising, and alveolar hemorrhage in the lungs.
citation: Page 76 (Book Page): [Primary effect is direct impact of steep pressure wave’s front... pressure waves cross it and produce shearing movement... causing it to be bruised... alveolar hemorrhage.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Differentiate between Retrograde and Anterograde post-traumatic amnesia.
back: Retrograde: Memory loss for events before the injury. Anterograde: Memory loss for events following the injury.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Antrograde amnesia extending forwards from the time of injury; Retrograde amnesia extending backwards from the time of regaining of consciousness.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of Tardieu's spots (petechial hemorrhages) in asphyxia.
back: Anoxia increases capillary permeability and causes vessel wall rupture, leading to small blood leaks under serous surfaces.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Anoxia also increases permeability of capillary wall forcing fluid out... Capillaries eventually rupture causing blood leaks... These petechial hemorrhages... Tardieu’s spots.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Q: Which laryngeal structures are most commonly fractured during manual strangulation?
back: The greater cornua of the hyoid bone and the superior horns of the thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fracture are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when they are calcified.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Define the pathological concept of a wound or injury in forensic medicine.
back: A wound or injury is defined as any break in body tissue, occurring either externally or internally, as a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): From medical point of view. any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How does weapon velocity specifically influence the kinetic energy of injury production?
back: Velocity dictates kinetic energy (K.E.=1/2mv²). Higher velocity weapons produce disproportionately greater destruction through phenomena like cavitation and energy radiation.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv². A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Contrast the histological margins of incised wounds versus lacerated wounds.
back: Incised: Clean-cut margins, sharp angles, smooth walls. Lacerated: Irregular margins, ill-defined angles, and bridging tissue tags/crushed hair bulbs.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): It shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls... Table 6.4: Lacerated Wound: Margins Irregular; Walls bridging of tissue; Angles ill defined.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Explain the mechanism behind a 'black eye' occurring 24 hours after a forehead strike.
back: Blood from a forehead bruise shifts via gravity along tissue lines of least resistance toward the lax periorbital tissue.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to lower region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Which histochemical markers differentiate ante-mortem from post-mortem skin burns?
back: Increased enzyme reactions (Alkaline/Acid phosphatase, leucine amino-peptidase) at the burn periphery indicate vital reaction absent in post-mortem burns.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn... Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the classic 'triad' of injury findings in secondary blast effects?
back: Secondary effects from flying debris cause a triad of circular bruises, abrasions, and small lacerations (dirt tattooing).
citation: Page 77 (Book Page): Injury characteristics are either in the form of dirt tattooing or triad of bruises, abrasions and small lacerations.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the 'local deformation' mechanism causing depressed skull fractures.
back: Impact creates a shallow cone; the apex stretches and fractures the inner table before the outer table breaks radially.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the outer table... fracture line in such depressed fracture tends to run radially.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Distinguish post-traumatic intra-cerebral hemorrhage from a spontaneous hypertensive stroke.
back: Traumatic: Usually frontal/temporal white matter in young victims. Spontaneous: Typically in basal ganglia regions of overweight, hypertensive individuals.
citation: Page 92 (Book Page): Location of post-traumatic hemorrhage is usually in white matter of frontal and temporal region... Spontaneous hemorrhage is usually in the ganglion regions.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Why is a head-to-foot electrical current pathway the most lethal?
back: This pathway involves the brain stem, containing vital cardiac and respiratory centers, precipitating immediate fatal inhibition.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): From head to either foot... involves brain stem having vital cardiac and respiratory centers is the most dangerous.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What threshold of intravascular air is required to cause fatal air embolism?
back: A volume of approximately 60 ml or more of air introduced into the circulation is sufficient to cause death.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): Volume of introduced air sufficient to cause death is about 60 ml or more.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What two primary factors determine the shape and appearance of a mechanical injury?
back:
1. Weapon Factors: Weight, velocity (Kinetic Energy = 1/2mv²), and manner of execution.
2. Part Struck Factors: Architecture (elasticity, density) and movement of the body part.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients... Weight and velocity ... Architecture of part struck with its behavior following a strike has specific relationship to the outcome.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiology of color changes in a bruise (contusion).
back:
Hemoglobin pigments change over time:
- Purple: Fresh (Deoxygenated blood).
- Greenish: 4–5 days (Enzymatic breakdown).
- Yellow: 7–10 days (Further degradation).
- Disappearance: 14–15 days.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Age of bruise is estimated from the color of effused blood... recent bruise appears purple... four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it turns yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Distinguish the microscopic features of an incised wound versus a lacerated wound.
back:
- Incised: Clean-cut margins, sharp angles, smooth walls, and hair bulbs cleanly cut.
- Lacerated: Irregular margins, bridging tissue tags, and crushed hair bulbs.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags... [Incised] shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls. If involved area is hair bearing, it shows cutting of hair including bulbs.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe Rowhbotham’s mechanism of 'Local Deformation' in skull fractures.
back: Impact creates a shallow cone. The apex stretches the inner table (fracturing first) while compressing the outer table. High force causes a comminuted depressed fracture.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Local deformation at the site occurs... Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the outer table... fracture confined to the inner-table at the apex of cone results.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the pathophysiology of 'Temporary Cavitation' in high-velocity bullet wounds?
back: High energy dissipates radially, pushing soft tissues laterally beyond the bullet's diameter. This creates an instant cavity larger than the projectile, followed by tissue recoil and collapse.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... creating instant cavitation... tissues recoil and collapse back leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Define 'Pugilistic Attitude' in a burnt corpse.
back: A specific 'boxer-like' posture caused by heat coagulation and shortening of the flexor muscle proteins. It occurs regardless of whether the burn was ante-mortem or post-mortem.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins. Finding has no significance, as even a dead body will attain it.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Compare the cardiac pathophysiology of low-voltage versus high-voltage electrical injuries.
back:
- Low Voltage: Myocardial fibrillation (disruption of pacemaker/conducting system).
- High Voltage: Spasmodic contraction and asystole (cardiac arrest).
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): [Low voltage produces myocardial fibrillation due to direct action on pace maker... High voltage either causes heart muscle to fibrillate or then becomes nonfunctional or produces spasmodic contraction and asystole.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the primary versus secondary effect in blast injury pathophysiology?
back:
- Primary: Direct impact of the high-speed over-pressure wave front.
- Secondary: Injuries from debris/missiles (primary or secondary) propelled by the blast.
citation: Page 76 (Book Page): [Primary effect is direct impact of steep pressure wave’s front... Secondary effect is an indirect consequence in the form of injuries received by the victims due to impact by debris energized by the blast.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Differentiate between Anterograde and Retrograde post-traumatic amnesia.
back:
- Anterograde: Memory loss extending forward in time from the moment of injury.
- Retrograde: Memory loss extending backward from the moment consciousness is regained.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic amnesia is of two types: Antrograde amnesia extending forwards from the time of injury [and] Retrograde amnesia extending backwards from the time of regaining of consciousness.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What are the three classic pathological stages of fatal asphyxia?
back:
1. Respiratory center stimulation (increased rate).
2. Struggled breathing (expiratory), cyanosis, and Tardieu's spots.
3. Coma, shallow/gasping breathing, and respiratory failure.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Phase I initiates stimulation of respiratory center... Phase II is characterized by struggle to breathe... Cyanosis deepens... Phase III is dominated by unconsciousness, which leads to coma. Breathing becomes irregular... Respiration finally fails.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
coreConcept: Age estimation of bruises via color changes
front: Q: What is the chronological sequence of color changes in the pathophysiology of a bruise?
back:
- Purple: 1-2 days (deoxygenated blood)
- Green: 4-5 days (hemoglobin breakdown)
- Yellow: 7-10 days (bilirubin/biliverdin)
- Disappears: ~2 weeks
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Color changes depend upon ability of the tissue to absorb it. Capillary blood is dark red in color and a recent bruise appears purple in color; it darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed. Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish. Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption of blood, and within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How does gravity influence the clinical presentation of deep-seated bruises?
back:
- Extravasated blood moves along tissue lines of least resistance under gravity.
- A blow to the forehead may manifest as a "black eye" within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to dependent region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Contrast the pathophysiology of antemortem versus postmortem wounds.
back:
- Antemortem: Shows "Vital Reaction" (hemorrhage, swelling, inflammatory response).
- Postmortem: Lacks vital reaction; no blood flow or cellular infiltration occurs.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion... Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.] Page 57 (Book Page): [Importance in distinction lies in the fact that bruising is an ante-mortem phenomenon indicating violence before death.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the systemic pathophysiological stages of fatal thermal burns.
back:
1. Primary shock (immediate): Due to intense pain.
2. Secondary shock (24-36 hrs): Fluid loss and hemoconcentration.
3. Delayed: Toxemia or infection/septicemia.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Chronological order of thermal burn complications upon the body as a whole are: Immediate primary shock due to pain; Secondary shock with circulatory collapse due to loss of fluid and hemo-concentration; Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia... or after many days, due to infection and septicemia.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Which biochemical markers detect antemortem burns before histological changes appear?
back:
- Increased enzyme activity at burn periphery.
- Specifically: Alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, and non-specific esterase.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Histo-chemistry at the periphery of the burnt skin indicates increased enzymes reaction... alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase... which can be detected much earlier than histological changes.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the defining histological criteria for the initiation of wound repair?
back:
- Invasion of white blood cells (leukocyte infiltration) at the site of injury.
- Becomes visible microscopically within 4 to 6 hours.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [The first form of vital reaction is initiation of the process of repair. It becomes visible microscopically within four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How does extensive mechanical crushing of limbs lead to renal failure?
back:
- Condition: Crush Syndrome.
- Pathophysiology: Renal ischemia combined with tubular obstruction by myoglobin and granular casts from damaged muscle.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Crush syndrome... Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney... This is associated with swelling and rupture of epithelium and eventual renal failure. It is suggested that it is due to... renal ischemia.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Differentiate the pathophysiology of fat embolism from air embolism.
back:
- Fat Embolism: Crushed adipose tissue/bone marrow enters circulation; fatal via pulmonary obstruction.
- Air Embolism: Suction of air into veins (min 60ml); fatal via cardiac tamponade/frothy blood.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Fat embolism follows trauma to the body, more so in crushing of the limbs... lungs show presence of fat droplets in pulmonary vessels.] Page 83 (Book Page): [Air embolism... Volume of introduced air sufficient to cause death is about 60 ml or more... fatal due to cardiac tamponade.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What physiological loop causes instantaneous death during manual throttling?
back:
- Vago-inhibitory reflex.
- Mechanism: Pressure on the carotid sinus/vagus nerve stimulates the parasympathetic system, causing sudden cardiac arrest.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): [Passage of electric current through spinal cord cause injury to cardiac and respiratory centers.] Page 150 (Book Page): [Death by vagal inhibition resultant from pressure over carotid sinus or vagus nerve... is immediate.] Page 154 (Book Page): [Reflex cardiac asystole takes place due to variations of tension within carotid sinuses.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How does tissue architecture determine the morphological type of internal injury?
back:
- Solid organs (liver/spleen): Rupture easily.
- Spongy organs (lungs): Sustain contusions.
- Hollow organs (heart/bladder): May burst if filled with fluid.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid; Lungs are spongy... Stomach, intestine, heart... are hollow sacs having fluid... a strike with a club... will produce different shaped injuries... due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: Any break in the continuity of body tissue, occurring either externally (skin) or internally (membranes/organs).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the biochemical mechanism of color changes in a bruise.
back: 1. Purple: Recent extravasation. 2. Greenish (4-5 days): Hemoglobin conversion to pigments via tissue enzymes. 3. Yellow: Final absorption stage.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Contrast the margins of an incised wound versus a lacerated wound.
back: Incised: Clean-cut margins and sharp angles. Lacerated: Irregular margins with characteristic bridging tissue tags.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What occurs when a high-velocity bullet strikes soft tissue?
back: It creates a temporary cavitation effect, dissipating high energy radially and causing damage significantly larger than the bullet's diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): High velocity bullet, on the other hand, additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How does carbon monoxide (CO) physiologically induce fatal anoxia?
back: CO has 200-300 times higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, forming stable carboxy-hemoglobin and halting oxygen transport.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): CO has 200-300 times affinity for hemoglobin than O2... It combines with hemoglobin to form carboxy-hemoglobin.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: List the four general pathological hallmarks of death by asphyxia.
back: 1. Generalized cyanosis. 2. Vascular congestion. 3. Edema. 4. Petechial (Tardieu's) hemorrhages.
citation: Page 75 (Book Page): General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis; Vascular congestion; Edema of the tissues and viscera; Petechial hemorrhages.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Why might a scalp injury result in a 'black eye' 24 hours later?
back: Due to gravity shifting, where extravasated blood moves along tissue lines of least resistance to the lax peri-orbital region.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Distinguish between antemortem and postmortem burns using vital reaction.
back: Antemortem burns show a red demarcating line, leucocyte infiltration, or high enzyme (alkaline phosphatase) activity at the periphery.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn... can be detected much earlier than histological changes.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Explain the physiological loop leading to renal failure in Crush Syndrome.
back: Muscle crushing releases myoglobin, which causes renal ischemia and blocks kidney tubules with granular casts.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney... associated with swelling and rupture of epithelium and eventual renal failure.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the Defining anatomical feature of a 'hesitation cut' in suicide?
back: Multiple, superficial, parallel skin cuts located near the initiation point of a deeper, lethal wound.
citation: Page 79 (Book Page): Self-inflicted cuts... are multiple, arranged parallel to each other and on the accessible parts of the body.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What are the four general pathological hallmarks of fatal asphyxia?
back: 1. Intense cyanosis. 2. Marked vascular congestion. 3. Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots). 4. Persistent fluidity of blood.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [General pathological changes in asphyxia • Generalized cyanosis • Vascular congestion • Edema of the tissues and viscera • Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera • Fluidity of blood]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of cavitation in high-velocity firearm wounds.
back: Kinetic energy dissipates radially into surrounding tissues, creating a momentary, temporary cavity significantly larger than the bullet's actual diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... tends to dissipate in the surrounding tissues more effectively in radial fashion creating instant cavitation. Period of cavitation is extremely short and soon after the passage of the bullet, tissues recoil and collapse back leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Differentiate the pathophysiology of a bruise from post-mortem hypostasis.
back: 1. Bruise: Extravasated blood in tissue spaces (not washable), shows swelling and vital reaction. 2. Hypostasis: Intravascular blood, shifts with gravity, washes away easily.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (Anti-mortem) 1. Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue... Hypostasis... Blood is within the vessels and when incised, it flows from the cut mouths of the blood vessels]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: A victim hit by a vehicle forgets events just before impact. Identify this pathophysiology.
back: Retrograde amnesia: Loss of memory for the period immediately preceding a brain trauma or loss of consciousness, often seen in concussive injuries.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic amnesia is of two types • Antrograde amnesia extending forwards from the time of injury • Retrograde amnesia extending backwards from the time of regaining of consciousness.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Why is Naloxone the physiological choice for reversing opioid injury?
back: It acts as a pure narcotic antagonist at receptor sites, effectively reversing respiratory depression, coma, and convulsions without agonist effects.
citation: Page 169 (Book Page): [Naloxone is a pure narcotic antagonist and is the recommended drug of choice for reversal of overdose doses of narcotic analgesics, particularly in the presence of respiratory depression, coma and convulsions.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What defines the diagnostic criteria for an ante-mortem burn?
back: 1. Redness (marginal hyperemia). 2. Blisters containing high-protein (albuminous) fluid. 3. Histological presence of leukocyte infiltration.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.6: Naked eye... Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening... Pressure steam and liquids... cause blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin... Microscopy... Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of an inner-table skull fracture during local impact.
back: Impact creates a shallow cone; the inner table is stretched (under tension) at the apex and fractures before the outer table.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the outer table... a fracture confined to the inner-table at the apex of cone results.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Differentiate a scalp "split laceration" from an incised wound.
back: Split lacerations have irregular margins, tissue bridging, and crushed hair bulbs, whereas incised wounds have cleanly severed edges and no bridging.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins... walls that have bridging tissue tags... bulbs of hair... forced into the surrounding tissue... crushed.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the physiological events characterizing Phase II of fatal asphyxia.
back: Struggle to breathe (expiratory effort), deep cyanosis, engorgement of neck veins, generalized vascular congestion, and systemic petechial hemorrhages.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Phase II is characterized by struggle to breathe, which starts with expiratory type of breathing. Cyanosis deepens with engorgement of neck veins. Generalized congestion and petechial hemorrhages start appearing.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Contrast the mode of death in low-voltage vs. high-voltage electrical injuries.
back: 1. Low Voltage: Ventricular/myocardial fibrillation. 2. High Voltage: Respiratory center paralysis or cardiac asystole (spasmodic contraction).
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): [i) Low voltage produces myocardial fibrillation due to direct action on pace maker... ii) High voltage either causes heart muscle to fibrillate... or produces spasmodic contraction and asystole.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: Any break in the body tissue, externally or internally. Both terms are considered synonymous in meaning and represent a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism causes a bruise to turn green after four to five days?
back: Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments like biliverdin and bilirubin as the body attempts to absorb effused blood.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Distinguish the physical characteristics of incised wound margins from lacerated wound margins.
back: * Incised: Clean cut margins, sharp angles, and smooth walls. * Lacerated: Irregular margins, ill-defined angles, and bridging tissue tags.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [It shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls.] and Page 57 (Book Page): [irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiology of a "black eye" appearing 24 hours after a forehead strike.
back: This is gravity shifting. Effused blood tracks along tissue lines of least resistance to dependent regions under gravitational influence within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to dependent region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Which specific enzymes increase at the periphery of an ante-mortem burn for early detection?
back: * Alkaline phosphatase * Acid phosphatase * Leucine amino-peptidase * Non-specific esterase.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Leucine amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: According to the Rule of Nine, what percentage of body surface is assigned to each upper limb?
back: Each upper limb (including the arm, forearm, and hand) is assigned 9% of the total body surface area.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Arm, forearm and hand of right side 9% Arm, forearm and hand of left side 9%]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What is the defining feature of a "metallization" lesion in electrical injuries?
back: The embedding of metallic particles, liberated from the conductor by a spark, into the superficial cells of the epidermis.
citation: Page 66 (Book Page): [showing multiple pricked or pitted metallization with metallic particles liberated from the conductor, which get embedded in the tissue.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: How does high-velocity bullet pathophysiology differ from low-velocity bullet pathophysiology regarding cavitation?
back: High-velocity bullets produce temporary cavitation by dissipating energy radially, resulting in permanent tissue damage much larger than the bullet's diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues... creating instant cavitation... leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: Describe the primary effect mechanism in a bomb blast injury.
back: It is the direct impact of the steep pressure wave front, acting as a blunt force that can lacerate tissues or cause mutilation.
citation: Page 76 (Book Page): [Primary effect is direct impact of steep pressure wave’s front... Pressure wave’s front acts like those of blunt force and produce injuries.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of injuries
front: Q: What physiological process causes the "pugilistic attitude" in a burnt corpse?
back: Heat-induced coagulation of muscle proteins and subsequent shortening of the flexor muscles, resulting in a characteristic boxer-like pose.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What sequence of color changes occurs in a bruise over time?
back: Purple (fresh) → Darkens (2 days) → Greenish (4-5 days) → Yellowish (7-10 days) → Disappears (2-3 weeks).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish. Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption of fluid, and within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two to three weeks]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of tissue damage in high-velocity bullet cavitation.
back: Dissipates energy radially, creating temporary cavitation. Tissues collapse back, leaving a permanent cavity larger than the bullet diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues... Period of cavitation is extremely short and soon after the passage of the bullet, tissues recoil and collapse back leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What microscopic and naked-eye features distinguish ante-mortem from post-mortem burns?
back: Naked-eye: Red line (1/4 inch) bordering lesion. Microscopy: Leukocyte infiltration and increased enzyme reaction (Alkaline Phosphatase) at the periphery.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion... Microscopy... Histo-chemistry at the periphery of the burn skin indicates increased enzymes reaction]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the clinical triad and histological finding in Crush Syndrome?
back: Triad: Muscle crushing, myoglobinuria, and renal failure. Histology: Myoglobin and granular casts in renal tubules.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Crush syndrome... Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney... This is associated with swelling and rupture of epithelium and eventual renal failure.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: How does Carbon Monoxide (CO) lead to cellular anoxia?
back: CO has 200-300x higher affinity than O2 for hemoglobin, forming carboxy-hemoglobin which inactivates O2 transport.
citation: Page 187 (Book Page): [CO has 200-300 times more affinity for hemoglobin than O2... It combines with hemoglobin to form carboxy-hemoglobin... It does not take part in O2 transport and thus produce symptom of O2 deprivations]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Define Tardieu's spots and their diagnostic significance.
back: Petechial hemorrhages under serous organ coverings (e.g., lungs, heart). Significance: Classical general pathological sign of asphyxia.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [These petechial hemorrhages were noticed first by Tardieu... They occur in the substance of the organs, but are more readily seen under their serous coverings... petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Distinguish between postmortem hypostasis and contact flattening.
back: Hypostasis: Purple-red discoloration in dependent parts. Contact flattening: White/pale areas where pressure prevents capillary filling.
citation: Page 134 (Book Page): [Any pressure anywhere on the body, however slight, will prevent the capillaries from filling and that is why pressure areas... do not show hypostasis.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast suicidal and homicidal cut-throat injuries based on wound characteristics.
back: Suicidal: High-up, hesitation cuts, tailing toward working hand. Homicidal: Lower, deep, bold, horizontal, no hesitation cuts.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): [Suicidal: Near initiation point, Hesitation cut, High up, Tailing present. Homicidal: Absent hesitation cut, Middle of neck, Boldly placed, Equidistant depth.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What physiological mechanism causes immediate death during neck compression?
back: Vagal Inhibition: Stimulation of carotid sinus or vagus nerve leads to sudden reflex cardiac arrest.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Carotid sinus/vagus nerve, which gets stimulated and precipitates reflex cardiac arrest... Vagal inhibition and sudden arrest of heart occurs almost instantaneous]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What are the defining characteristics of a lacerated wound?
back: Irregular margins, ill-defined angles, and the presence of bridging tissue tags or crushed hair bulbs.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags and hair... bulbs of hair are crushed]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: A: Any break in the body tissue, occurring either externally or internally.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What unique damage mechanism is produced by a high-velocity bullet in soft tissue?
back: A: Temporary cavitation. The high kinetic energy causes tissues to displace radially, leaving a permanent cavity larger than the bullet diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): High velocity bullet, on the other hand, additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally over and above the damage caused by the low velocity bullet.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Distinguish antemortem bruises from postmortem pseudo-bruising.
back:
1. Antemortem: Shows vital reaction (swelling/inflammation) and extravasation.
2. Postmortem: Lacks vital reaction; usually due to shifted hypostasis.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Importance in distinction lies in the fact that bruising is an ante- mortem phenomenon indicating violence before death. [Table 1.3: Bruise (anti-mortem) ... Presence of vital reaction]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Describe the characteristic features of a rifled firearm entry wound.
back:
1. Circular hole with inverted margins.
2. Marginal abrasion ring.
3. Possible peripheral stamping (smoke, soot, or tattooing) depending on distance.
citation: Page 71 (Book Page): Riffled weapon entry wound is typically circular hole with inverted margins like poking of a lead pencil through skin.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Which biochemical markers differentiate antemortem from postmortem burns?
back: A: Increased enzyme reactions at the burn periphery, specifically alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, and non-specific esterase.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): Histo-chemistry at the periphery of the burn skin indicates increased enzymes reaction... alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What are the three defining histological hallmarks of a lacerated wound?
back:
1. Irregular margins.
2. Bridging tissue tags (nerves/vessels).
3. Crushing or bruising of the wound edges.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: In forensic burn assessment, what is the 'Rule of Nine' used to calculate?
back: A: The extent and percentage of the total body surface area (TBSA) involved in the thermal injury.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): During forensic certification, Medical Examiner takes advantage of the rule of nine to calculate the extent and percentage area involved bearing burns.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast the wound depth of suicidal vs. homicidal cutthroat injuries.
back:
1. Suicidal: Deepest at the initiation point, often with 'hesitation cuts.'
2. Homicidal: Usually uniform depth and boldly placed without hesitation marks.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): [Table 7.5: Feature ... Depth of wound ... Suicidal: Maximum at the point of initiation ... Homicidal: Maximum in the middle]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Explain the physiological 'air lock' mechanism in fatal venous air embolism.
back: A: Air enters damaged veins, travels to the right ventricle, and obstructs blood flow to the lungs, precipitating immediate circulatory collapse.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): Postmortem appearance is characteristic showing presence of a chain of bubbles in the neck. Coronary veins and on opening the heart its right side is filled with frothy blood.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What are Tardieu's spots, and where are they most commonly found?
back: A: Small petechial hemorrhages occurring under the serous coverings of internal organs (lungs, heart) due to capillary rupture in asphyxia.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): These petechial hemorrhages were noticed first by Tardieu and are identified with his name as Tardieu’s spots. They occur in the substance of the organs, but are more readily seen under their serous coverings.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: How does the law define 'injury' regarding the human body?
back:
* Any harm caused illegally to a person in:
1. Body
2. Mind
3. Reputation
4. Property.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of a 'black eye' following a forehead injury.
back:
* Blood from the forehead injury shifts downward under the influence of gravity within 24 hours.
* It pools in the lax subcutaneous tissues surrounding the eyes.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site... under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours... noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the primary histological distinction between a bruise and postmortem lividity?
back:
* Bruise: Extra-vascular blood (outside vessels) due to tissue rupture.
* Lividity: Intra-vascular blood (contained within vessels).
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise: Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in inter-statius tissue... Postmortem Lividity: Blood is within the vessels.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Why does a high-velocity bullet cause explosive disintegration of fluid-filled organs?
back:
* Kinetic energy causes temporary cavitation.
* Fluid is displaced explosively in all directions, behaving as 'secondary projectiles' that disorganize surrounding tissues.
citation: Page 73 (Book Page): [When high velocity bullet... hits... fluid... its contents get separated into particles, which get displaced explosively in all directions away from the bullet path and behave as secondary projectiles.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the specific pharmacological intervention for organophosphate insecticide poisoning?
back:
* Atropine Sulfate: Blockades acetylcholine at neuroreceptors.
* Dose: 1-2mg IV, repeated every 5 minutes until secretions cease.
citation: Page 173 (Book Page): [In case of organo-phosphate poisoning... Atropine sulfate... 1 to 2mg... repeated intravenously at five minute intervals until toxic symptoms of atropine become manifest.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What percentage of total body surface area is allocated to the head and neck in burns?
back:
* 9%.
* This includes the face, neck, and scalp.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Face, neck and scalp 9%]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Explain the cause of the 'pugilistic attitude' in a burnt corpse.
back:
* It is caused by heat coagulation of muscle proteins.
* Shortening of the flexor muscles forces limbs into a boxer-like pose.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast the character of suicidal versus homicidal cut-throat wounds.
back:
* Suicidal: Superficial 'hesitation cuts' present; deepest at initiation point.
* Homicidal: Bold, deep, uniform wounds in the middle of the neck; hesitation marks absent.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [Table 7.5: Suicidal: Hesitation cut present... Maximum [depth] at point of initiation... Homicidal: Hesitation cut absent... Boldly placed in the center... Maximum [depth] in the middle.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop leading to renal failure in 'Crush Syndrome'.
back:
* Muscle crushing releases myoglobin into circulation.
* Myoglobin and granular casts block renal tubules.
* This, combined with renal ischemia, causes acute renal failure.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Crush syndrome... Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney... due to renal ischemia... eventual renal failure.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the earliest microscopic sign of a 'vital reaction' in a tissue injury?
back:
* Invasion of white blood cells (leukocytes).
* Occurs within 4 to 6 hours after the injury in living tissue.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells into the site of injury.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: Any break in body tissue, occurring either externally or internally. In pathology, both terms are considered synonymous.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What biochemical process causes a bruise to turn greenish in 4-5 days?
back: Tissue enzymes begin converting hemoglobin into blood pigments. This follows the initial purple stage of effused blood darkening.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Differentiate antemortem bruises from post-mortem pseudo-bruising.
back: Antemortem bruises show vital reactions (swelling/inflammation). The blood is extravasated into interstitial tissue rather than just pooling in vessels.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (Anti-mortem) - Vital reaction (swelling and inflammation) present... Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Why does a blunt strike to the scalp often resemble an incised wound?
back: This is a split (crush) laceration. Skin is crushed against underlying bone, causing a linear breach with minimal marginal bruising.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues between the weapon and the underlying bone split them. It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Why does blood remain fluid in sudden, unexpected deaths?
back: Sudden emotional stress triggers the vascular endothelium to secrete fibrinolysin. This enzyme dissolves clots within 15-30 minutes.
citation: Page 134 (Book Page): [It stimulated production of fibrinolysin by vascular endothelium into blood circulation, which dissolved the already formed clot. This change kept the blood in fluid state.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the volume threshold for immediate fatal hemorrhage?
back: Rapid loss of one-third of the total body blood volume is generally sufficient to cause immediate death.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [Rapid loss of blood, one third of the body is sufficient to cause immediate death in general terms.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: How is the age of an open infected wound estimated by discharge?
back: Sero-purulent discharge appears in 3-4 days. This is followed by red-granulation tissue formation in 5-6 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [appearance of sero-purulent discharge in about three to four days, followed by formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast high-velocity vs. low-velocity bullet effects on soft tissue.
back: Low-velocity bullets cause lateral energy radiation. High-velocity bullets create temporary cavitation, resulting in permanent cavities larger than the bullet diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues... leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop causing death in carotid sinus pressure.
back: Increased tension triggers strong parasympathetic stimulation. This produces reflex circulatory inhibition, slowing the pulse and stopping the heart.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Increased tension... precipitates strong parasympathetic stimulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse... resulting in reflex cardiac arrest.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What causes the "Pugilistic Attitude" in a burnt corpse?
back: Heat-induced coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins. It occurs regardless of whether the burn was antemortem.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: Medical definition: Any break in body tissue, externally or internally. Pathologically, wound and injury are synonymous entities.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What characterizes the mechanism of a moving abrasion (graze)?
back:
Mechanism:
- Friction removes the epidermis
- Causes heaping/piling of tissue at the far end
- Indicates direction of force
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end. Appearance is characteristic.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: How do bruises and postmortem lividity differ in blood location?
back:
Contrast:
- Bruise: Blood is in inter-statius tissue (extravascular)
- Lividity: Blood remains within vessels (intravascular)
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Bruise (Anti-mortem)... Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in blood surrounding inter-statius tissue... Post-mortem Lividity... Blood is within the vessels and when incised, blood flows out.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Explain the clinical mechanism of a 'black eye' after forehead trauma.
back: Mechanism: Gravitational shifting of effused blood from the forehead site along tissue lines of least resistance, occurring within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to lower region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Which enzymes increase at the periphery of antemortem skin burns?
back:
Key Enzymes:
- Alkaline phosphatase
- Acid phosphatase
- Lucien amino-peptidase
- Non-specific esterase
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn... Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: According to the Rule of Nine, what percentage represents one entire lower limb?
back: Total per limb: 18%. (9% for the front of the thigh/leg and 9% for the back of the thigh/leg).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): Front of thigh, leg & foot of right side 9%; Back of thigh, leg & sole of foot of right side 9%.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Describe the 'temporary cavitation' effect caused by high-velocity bullets.
back: High kinetic energy dissipates radially, creating an instant cavity in soft tissues that collapses, leaving damage much larger than the bullet diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... creating instant cavitation... leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Differentiate suicidal and homicidal cutthroat wounds based on 'hesitation cuts'.
back: Suicide: Multiple superficial hesitation cuts present at the initiation point. Homicide: Hesitation cuts are characteristically absent.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): Table 7.5... Hesitation cut: Suicidal: Near initiation point. Homicidal: Absent.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What metabolic mechanism causes 'Crush Syndrome' renal failure?
back: Mechanism: Muscle necrosis releases myoglobin and acid metabolites, causing renal ischemia and obstruction of kidney tubules by granular casts.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): Crush syndrome... Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney... due to renal ischemia and not to mechanical obstruction by casts etc.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Which specific laryngeal structures are prone to fracture in throttling?
back: Common sites: The greater cornua of the hyoid bone and the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Define "Hurt" according to the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ or body part without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism causes muscle stiffening in Rigor Mortis?
back: Decomposition of Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) prevents actin and myosin from dissociating, resulting in a permanent rigid gel cross-link.
citation: Page 134 (Book Page): [After death, adenosine triphosphate of the muscles decomposes. Both the actin and myosin become stiff and get converted into a rigid gel... this state of muscles is called rigor mortis.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast the margins of an entry wound versus an exit wound in rifled firearms.
back:
Entry Wound: Inverted margins (typically smaller than the bullet). 
Exit Wound: Everted margins (usually larger and more irregular).
citation: Page 74 (Book Page): [Character: Smaller or equal (Entry), Larger (Exit)... Margins: inverted (Entry), everted (Exit)]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: A victim presents with a scalp wound showing bridging tissue tags. Interpret the injury type.
back: Lacerated wound (specifically a split/crush laceration); bridging tissue and irregular margins distinguish it from sharp-edged incised wounds.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins... that have bridging tissue tags.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the significance of 'Marbling' during putrefaction?
back: Sulfurated hydrogen reacts with hemoglobin in superficial veins, producing green/black sulfmethemoglobin that traces a vascular pattern on the skin.
citation: Page 136 (Book Page): [The green color changes to blackish brown and veins in these areas become prominent and visible due to accumulation of gases in them due to decomposition and shows marbling stage.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: List the diagnostic hallmarks of fatal Asphyxia.
back:
1. Generalized cyanosis
2. Vascular congestion
3. Edema of viscera
4. Tardieu’s spots (petechial hemorrhages)
5. Fluidity of blood.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Table 13.1: General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema of the tissues and viscera, Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera, Fluidity of blood.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Calculate the 'Rule of Nine' percentage for burns involving the entire right arm.
back: 9% total (Includes arm, forearm, and hand).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Arm, forearm and hand of right side: 9%]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Differentiate a 'Contusion' from 'Post-mortem Lividity' (Hypostasis).
back:
Contusion: Blood is in interstitial tissue (won't wash away); shows vital reaction. 
Lividity: Blood is intravascular; depends on gravity/pressure.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (Anti-mortem): Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue... Post-mortem Lividity: Blood is within the vessels.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Describe the color change sequence in a healing bruise.
back: Purple (Recent) → Greenish (4–5 days) → Yellow (7–10 days) → Fading.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [A recent bruise appears purple... in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What are 'Tardieu's spots' and where are they most visible?
back: Petechial hemorrhages caused by capillary rupture due to anoxia; most readily seen under serous coverings of organs (e.g., pleura).
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [These petechial hemorrhages were noticed first by Tardieu... They occur in the substance of the organs, but are more readily seen under their serous coverings.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: Any break in the body tissue, occurring either externally or internally.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Describe the chronological color changes of a bruise due to hemoglobin degradation.
back:
• 0–2 days: Purple (oxygen removed)
• 4–5 days: Greenish (enzyme action)
• 7–10 days: Yellowish (absorption)
• Final: Disappears.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Color changes depend upon ability of the tissue to absorb it... a recent bruise appears purple in color... in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast an ante-mortem bruise with post-mortem lividity upon incision.
back:
• Bruise: Extravasated blood is in tissue spaces; does not wash away.
• Lividity: Blood is within vessels; washes away easily with water.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (Anti-mortem) Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue... Lividity (Post-mortem) Blood is present within the vessels and when incised, can be washed away.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: A victim with severe leg crushing develops renal failure. Explain the underlying pathology.
back:
• Condition: Crush Syndrome.
• Cause: Renal ischemia and excretion of acid metabolites.
• Finding: Myoglobin pigments and granular casts in kidney tubules.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Crush syndrome... is due to renal ischemia... Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney. This is associated with swelling and rupture of tubular epithelium and eventual renal failure.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Which specific injuries are most commonly associated with fatal fat embolism?
back: Crushing of the limbs, particularly when associated with damage to bones and adipose (fatty) tissue.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Fat embolism... occurs following trauma to the body, more so in crushing injuries of the limbs especially when associated with fractures of bones and soft tissues like muscles and adipose tissue.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
