front: Q: What are the primary diagnostic criteria for an ante-mortem burn?
back:
• Hyperemia: Line of redness bordering the lesion.
• Blisters: Contain plasma exudate rich in albumin.
• Histology: Leucocyte infiltration.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.6: Naked eye Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion... Microscopy Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: How is the 'Rule of Nine' applied to calculate the surface area of both upper limbs?
back: Total 18% (9% for the right arm, forearm, and hand; 9% for the left side).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Arm, forearm and hand of right side 9% Arm, forearm and hand of left side 9%]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Differentiate between an incised wound and a split laceration on the scalp.
back:
• Incised: Clean-cut margins, hair bulbs cut, no bridging tissue.
• Split Laceration: Irregular margins, bridging tissue tags, hair bulbs crushed.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Split laceration... Hair bulbs of hairs are crushed. Denudation of hair in a hair bearing area may occur... Table 6.4: Incised Wound Clean cut margins... bridging tissues absent... Hair Bulbs Cleanly cut.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of death in fatal air embolism following injury.
back: Air enters venous circulation, reaches the right heart/pulmonary artery, and blocks flow. Lethal volume is 60 ml or more.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [Air embolism... enters into circulation... negative pressure in the veins are responsible. Volume of introduced air sufficient to cause death is about 60 ml or more.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What are the three mechanical types of abrasions used in forensic identification?
back:
1. Moving (Graze/Scratch)
2. Imprint (Contact pattern)
3. Friction.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [There are of three types: Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: A: Any break in body tissue, whether external or internal. Both terms are considered synonymous pathological entities in medical practice.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): From medical point of view. any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of a 'split' or 'crush' laceration.
back: A: Caused by sudden compression of skin against underlying bone. It occurs on areas where skin is firmly supported, such as the scalp or chin.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Split laceration occurs on scalp, forehead, chin or any other part of the body where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues betweenn the weapon and the underlying bone split them.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast the characteristics of incised wounds versus lacerated wounds.
back:
A: 
- Incised: Clean-cut margins, sharp angles, smooth walls.
- Lacerated: Irregular margins, bruised edges, bridging tissue tags, and crushed hair bulbs.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Lacerated] Irregular [margins]... Ill defined [angles]... bridging tissue tags. [Incised] Clean cut [margins]... sharp [angles]... smooth [walls].

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: A victim develops a 'black eye' 24 hours after a forehead strike. Name this process.
back: A: Gravity shifting of a bruise. Extravasated blood moves along tissue lines of least resistance under the influence of gravity to lower regions.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity ... noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: List the specific enzymes used in histochemistry to identify ante-mortem burns.
back:
A: 
- Alkaline phosphatase
- Acid phosphatase
- Leucine amino-peptidase
- Non-specific esterase
Increased reaction at the periphery indicates vital response.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase. ... Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What are the sequential color changes used to estimate the age of a bruise?
back:
A: 
- Fresh: Purple/Dark Red
- 4-5 Days: Greenish
- 7-10 Days: Yellow
- 2 Weeks: Disappears
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): recent bruise appears purple in color ... in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish ... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Differentiate the primary and secondary wounding effects of high-velocity bullets.
back:
A: 
- Primary: Perforation proportionate to bullet diameter.
- Secondary: Temporary cavitation pushing tissues laterally, leaving a cavity much larger than the projectile diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): High velocity bullet ... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally ... leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Distinguish between the primary, secondary, and tertiary effects of a bomb blast.
back:
A: 
- Primary: Direct pressure wave impact (over-pressure).
- Secondary: Impact from flying debris and missiles.
- Tertiary: Victim propelled against walls or solid barriers.
citation: Page 76 (Book Page)-78: Primary effect is direct impact of steep pressure wave’s front ... Secondary effect is an indirect consequence ... due to impact by debris ... Tertiary effect is also an indirect injury caused to victims by his striking against a wall.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Explain the 'hold-on' versus 'throw-off' electrical effects based on voltage.
back:
A: 
- Hold-on (220-240V): Causes muscle spasm preventing release of live wire.
- Throw-off (600-1200V): Causes a single violent contraction that propels the victim away.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): ‘Hold-on effect’ at 220-240V (domestic) causes muscle spasm, responsible for non-release ... ‘Throw-off effect’ at 600V-1200V (industrial) single contraction of short period of contact.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Define a 'penetrating' wound in forensic trauma cases.
back: A: A wound from a sharp, pointed weapon that pierces a body cavity (cranium, chest, abdomen). Depth is the greatest dimension.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): Penetrating & puncturing wound is produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon into part of the body having a cavity like cranium, chest and abdomen which gets pierced.

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back:
- Any break in body tissue.
- Can occur either externally or internally.
- Pathologically, wound and injury are synonymous.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism drives the color changes in a maturing bruise?
back:
- Tissue enzymes break down hemoglobin.
- Hemoglobin converts into blood pigments (bilirubin/biliverdin).
- Progresses from purple (recent) to green (4-5 days) to yellow (7-10 days).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish. Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption of pigments... yellow and finally disappears.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast the margins and hair condition of incised versus lacerated wounds.
back:
- Incised: Clean-cut margins, sharp angles, hair bulbs cut cleanly.
- Lacerated: Irregular/bruised margins, bridging tissue tags, hair bulbs crushed.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [It shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls. If involved area is hair bearing, it shows cutting of hair including bulbs.] Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins... bridging tissue tags and hair... crushed.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: An elderly patient dies weeks after a femur fracture; list three secondary causes of death.
back:
- Pulmonary Embolism: From deep vein thrombosis.
- Bronchopneumonia: Due to prolonged immobility.
- Septicemia: From secondary infection of the injury site.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Secondary conditions like embolism, crush syndrome and bronchopneumonia may occur following trauma... Bronchopneumonia occurs in elderly persons following fractures of lower limbs and consequent immobility.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the pharmacological rationale for using Atropine in organo-phosphate poisoning?
back:
- Acts as a parasympatholytic agent.
- Blocks acetylcholine at the neuroreceptor site.
- Reverses muscarinic effects (salivation, bradycardia).
citation: Page 170 (Book Page): [Atropine sulfate is a parasympatholytic agent, which effectively blocks the effects of acetylcholine at the neuroreceptor site. The drug is indicated in treatment of symptoms of poisoning with organo-phosphate.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: List the four criteria used to estimate the severity of acute poisoning.
back:
- Degree of coma.
- Depth of respiratory depression.
- Extent of circulatory shock.
- Presence of hypothermia.
citation: Page 170 (Book Page): [Assessment of patient’s condition, regarding severity of acute poisoning should be done clinically from degree of coma, depth of respiratory depression, extent of shock and hypothermia.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: How is 'Reaction Time' impacted by alcohol in the context of transportation accidents?
back:
- Alcohol is a CNS depressant.
- It prolongs reaction time (e.g., from 0.1 to 0.5+ seconds).
- Impairs muscular coordination and power of decision.
citation: Page 93 (Book Page): [Alcohol, being a central nervous system depressant, prolongs reaction time and causes slowing of muscular coordination... driver... cannot control himself cannot control motor vehicle.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Differentiate firearm entry from exit wounds based on margin and blast imprints.
back:
- Entry: Inverted margins, smaller than bullet, fire-blast soot/tattooing often present.
- Exit: Everted margins, larger/irregular shape, fire-blast imprints absent.
citation: Page 74 (Book Page): [Table 7.2: Character: Entry: Smaller or equal... Exit: Larger. Margins: Entry: Inverted... Exit: Everted. Fire blast imprint: Entry: Present... Exit: Absent.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of death in low-voltage vs high-voltage electrical injuries.
back:
- Low-voltage: Death by ventricular fibrillation (direct action on pacemaker).
- High-voltage: Death by asystole or spasmodic heart muscle contraction.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): [i) Low voltage produces myocardial fibrillation due to direct action on pace maker... ii) High voltage... produces spasmodic contraction and asystole.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What findings differentiate ante-mortem burns from post-mortem burns?
back:
- Ante-mortem: Shows vital reaction (reddening, leukocyte infiltration, increased enzymes).
- Post-mortem: Lacks vital reaction; mimics parchment-like skin.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Ante-mortem burn recognition depends upon presence of vital reaction... Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening... Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the estimated age of a bruise when it appears greenish in color?
back: 4 to 5 days. This transition occurs as tissue enzymes begin breaking down hemoglobin into blood pigments.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What pathophysiological mechanism causes a bruise to darken within the first 48 hours?
back: Deoxygenation of the effused blood. Capillary blood is initially dark red but loses oxygen over two days.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [a recent bruise appears purple in color; it darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Differentiate the age of an abrasion based on soft versus hard scab formation.
back:
• Soft scab: Approximately 2 days.
• Hard scab: 3 to 4 days.
• Scab falls off: 4 to 7 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: An open wound bed displays red granulation tissue. What is the most likely age of this injury?
back: 5 to 6 days. This typically follows the swelling of margins and sero-purulent discharge.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the first microscopic histological sign used to determine the age of a vital wound?
back: Invasion of white blood cells (leukocytes) at the site of injury. This occurs within 4 to 6 hours.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What are the diagnostic criteria for a bruise that is 7 to 10 days old?
back: The bruise appears yellow. This is the final color stage before the bruise disappears entirely.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [fading of the bruise occurs... within seven to ten days, color becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Apply the timeline of healing to a clean, non-gaping incised wound during the first 36 hours.
back:
• Initial: Covered by lymph and blood.
• 24-36 Hours: Clotting is completed.
• 3-4 Days: Margins adhere.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping wound gets covered by lymph and blood, which clot in first twenty four to thirty six hours. It is followed by adherence of edges in about three to four days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Differentiate the healing of a septic vs. clean wound in terms of final scar formation.
back:
• Clean wound: Red linear scar at 12–14 days.
• Slightly septic wound: Fresh scar at 12–16 days (more prominent and raised).
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Process of healing is completed with red linear scar formation in about twelve to fourteen days... healing gets completed in twelve to sixteen days. Fresh scar in such a wound is more prominent and slightly raised]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Explain the metabolic loop responsible for the yellowing of a bruise.
back: Enzymatic degradation of hemoglobin into blood pigments like bilirubin and biliverdin, occurring as the tissue absorbs the effused blood.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, color becomes yellow]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the general anatomical rule for the total time required for a bruise to disappear?
back: Approximately 2 weeks. The exact duration varies based on the size, depth, and anatomical site of the injury.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [finally disappears in about two weeks; the time depends upon site, size and depth of the bruise.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the chronological color sequence of a bruise during the healing process?
back:
- 0-2 days: Purple/Dark red
- 4-5 days: Greenish
- 7-10 days: Yellowish
- 2 weeks: Total disappearance
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Age of bruise is estimated from the color of effused blood... Purple in color, darkens in two days... greenish in about four/five days... yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What specific mechanical mechanism produces a split (crush) laceration?
back:
- Sudden compression of skin between a weapon and underlying bone
- Common on scalp, chin, or forehead
- May visually mimic an incised wound
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split laceration occurs on scalp, forehead, chin... Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues between the weapon and the underlying bone split them.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: How are ante-mortem burns distinguished from post-mortem burns during examination?
back:
- Presence of a vital reaction (red line of demarcation)
- Blisters containing albumin-rich plasma exudate
- Presence of soot/carbon monoxide in the trachea
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Ante-mortem burn recognition depends upon presence of vital reaction... blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin... Presence of black sooty particles in trachea.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: A trauma victim shows a lucid interval before rapid deterioration. Which injury is suspected?
back:
- Extradural Hemorrhage (EDH)
- Rupture of middle meningeal artery/vein
- Typically associated with temporal fossa linear fractures
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Extradural hemorrhage... rupture of the middle meningeal artery or vein... most common site is temporal fossa... clinical history of a 'lucid interval'.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the primary pharmacological management for organophosphate insecticide poisoning?
back:
- Atropine sulfate: Blocks acetylcholine at neuroreceptor sites
- Repeated IV doses until secretions cease
- Gastric lavage if poison was ingested
citation: Page 170 (Book Page): [Atropine sulfate... effectively blocks the effects of acetylcholine at the neuroreceptor site. The drug is indicated in the treatment of poisoning with organophosphate insecticides.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What are the four classical internal autopsy findings of mechanical asphyxia?
back:
- Generalized cyanosis
- Intense visceral/vascular congestion
- Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots)
- Fluidity of blood
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [General pathological changes in asphyxia... Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema... Petechial hemorrhages... Fluidity of blood.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: How does weapon velocity exponentially increase injury severity based on kinetic energy?
back:
- K.E. = 1/2 mv² (velocity is squared)
- High-velocity projectiles cause massive tissue disintegration
- Temporary cavitation occurs in soft tissues
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv²... A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity... shall produce greater damage.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Contrast the ligature mark characteristics of hanging versus homicidal strangulation.
back:
- Hanging: Oblique, non-continuous, high in the neck
- Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous (complete loop), middle/lower neck
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Oblique, Incomplete... Strangulation: Horizontal, Complete.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: What is the physiological mechanism of Carbon Monoxide (CO) lethality?
back:
- CO has 200-300x higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen
- Forms stable carboxy-hemoglobin
- Inactivates oxygen transport, causing cellular anoxia
citation: Page 187 (Book Page): [CO has 200-300 times more affinity for hemoglobin than O2... combines with hemoglobin to form carboxy-hemoglobin... inactivates from carrying O2.]

category: Explain effects of injuries on the body
front: Q: Which specific injury type is most commonly associated with fatal fat embolism?
back:
- Crush injuries of limbs
- Fractures of long bones (e.g., femur)
- Release of marrow fat into venous circulation
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Fat embolism occurs as a result of trauma... more so in crushing of the limbs especially when associated with long bone fractures.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the chronological healing sequence for a skin abrasion?
back:
1. Soft scab (2 days)
2. Hard scab (3-4 days)
3. Scab retraction (subsequent 3-4 days)
4. Scab falls off.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon... formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Explain the color changes seen in a bruise as it ages.
back:
1. Purple (recent)
2. Dark/Blue (2 days)
3. Greenish (4-5 days)
4. Yellow (7-10 days)
5. Disappears (2-3 weeks).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [recent bruise appears purple in color; darkens in two days... four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two to three weeks.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Differentiate the margins of a fresh versus a slightly septic healing wound.
back:
Fresh: Covered by lymph/blood (24-36 hours).
Slightly Septic: Margin swelling (12-16 hours), sero-purulent discharge (3-4 days), red granulation (5-6 days).
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping wound gets covered by lymph and blood... in first twenty four to thirty six hours... Slightly septic wound margins swell in first twelve to sixteen hours, followed by... sero-purulent discharge in about three to four days... red-granulation tissue... in about five to six days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: A wound shows red granulation tissue in its bed. What is its approximate age?
back: Approximately 5 to 6 days. This occurs in slightly septic wounds following the stage of sero-purulent discharge.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [followed by formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: When do microscopic signs of wound repair first become visible?
back: Within four to six hours. It is characterized by the invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically within four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells in the site of injury.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: After how many days does a bruise typically acquire a greenish color?
back: Four to five days. This is caused by tissue enzymes converting hemoglobin into blood pigments.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the timeline for red linear scar formation in a non-gaping wound?
back: Seven to ten days. Initially, margins adhere by 3-4 days, followed by the formation of the fresh red scar.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [followed by adherence of margins in about three to four days. Process of healing is completed with red linear scar formation in about seven to ten days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How does repeated police battering affect the estimation of bruise age?
back: It accelerates darkening of effused blood to deep blue within hours rather than two days, mimicking older vital reactions.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [repeated strikes... interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and causes color change from first two days to few hours i.e. rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue color.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Describe the progression of a septic wound during the first 16 days.
back:
1. Swelling: 12-16 hrs
2. Discharge: 3-4 days
3. Granulation: 5-6 days
4. Healing/Scar: 12-16 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Slightly septic wound... margins swell in first twelve to sixteen hours... sero-purulent discharge in about three to four days... red-granulation tissue... in about five to six days, skin grows over it and healing gets completed in twelve to sixteen days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the typical duration for a bruise to disappear completely?
back: About two to three weeks. The specific duration depends on the site, size, and depth of the original injury.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [finally disappears in about two to three weeks, depending upon site, size and depth of the bruise.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the typical color progression used to estimate the age of a bruise?

• 2 Days: Darkens/Dark Blue
• 4 to 5 Days: Greenish
• 7 to 10 Days: Yellowish
• 2 Weeks: Disappears
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [A recent bruise appears purple in color; darkens in two days... in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism is responsible for the changing colors in an aging bruise?
back:
• Breakdown of hemoglobin by tissue enzymes into various blood pigments.
• Initial darkening occurs as oxygen is removed from the blood within two days.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed. Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How do scab changes in an abrasion indicate wound duration?
back:
• Soft Scab: ~2 days
• Hard Scab: 3–4 days after soft scab formation
• Retraction/Falling: 3–4 days after hardening (Total ~7–10 days)
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the estimated age of a clean, non-gaping wound showing a red linear scar?
back:
• Approximately 7 to 10 days.
• Follows initial clotting (24-36 hours) and edge adherence (3-4 days).
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Process of healing is completed with red linear scar formation in about seven to ten days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the earliest microscopic sign of vital reaction indicating wound age?
back:
• Invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.

citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically within four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What are the diagnostic criteria for aging a slightly septic wound at 3–4 days?
back:
• Appearance of sero-purulent discharge.

citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Slightly septic wound margins swell in first twelve to sixteen hours, followed by appearance of sero-purulent discharge in about three to four days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How is the presence of red-granulation tissue used to date a septic wound?
back:
• Indicates an age of approximately 5 to 6 days.
• Full healing typically completes by 12–16 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [followed by formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days... healing gets completed in twelve to sixteen days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How does 'Police Battering' (repeated strikes) affect the perceived age of a bruise?
back:

citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [repeated strikes to body part... causes rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue color. It should not be confused with vital reaction occurring with passage of time.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound

front: Q: What biological mechanism drives the color transitions in a bruise?
back: Tissue enzymes break down hemoglobin into various blood pigments over time.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Distinguish the healing timeline of clean versus slightly septic wounds.
back:
- Clean: Clot (24-36 hrs), edges adhere (3-4 days), red scar (7-10 days).

citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping... clot in first twenty four to thirty six hours... adherence of edges in about three to four days... slightly septic... sero-purulent discharge in about three to four days, followed by formation of red-granulation tissue... in about five to six days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound

back:
- Soft scab: 2 days.

citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

back: Invasion of white blood cells (leucocytes) at the site.

back: Approximately 7 to 10 days after the injury.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Process of healing is completed with red linear scar formation in about seven to ten days.]

citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs... under the influence of gravity within first few hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How does the presence of pus and granulation tissue affect age estimation?
back: It indicates a septic wound where granulation appears around day 5-6 and healing completes by day 12-16.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days, skin grows over it and healing gets completed in twelve to sixteen days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the standard timeframe for an ante-mortem bruise to disappear?
back: Generally two weeks, depending on its site, size, and depth.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Turns yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks. The time varies upon site, size and depth of the bruise.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What macroscopic features are used to estimate the age of an abrasion?
back:

- Soft scab formation (2 days).

- Scab retraction and falling off (7-10 days).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What pathophysiological process dictates the color changes used to age a bruise?
back: Tissue enzymes break down hemoglobin into various blood pigments (biliverdin, bilirubin) sequentially over two weeks, altering the visual color from purple to yellow.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Age of bruise is estimated from the color of effused blood... Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Contrast the appearance of a clean vs. septic open wound at 3-4 days post-injury.

citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping wound... followed by adherence of edges in about three to four days. Slightly septic wound margins swell... followed by appearance of sero-purulent discharge in about three to four days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: A wound shows white blood cell invasion under microscopy. What is the minimum estimated age?
back: The injury is at least 4 to 6 hours old, as this is the earliest interval for microscopic evidence of repair initiation.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [process of repair. It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism allows for dating wounds earlier than macroscopic changes?

citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Histo-chemistry at the periphery of the burnt skin indicates increased enzymes reaction... can be detected much earlier than histological changes.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound

citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping wound gets covered by lymph and blood, which clot in first twenty four to thirty six hours.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: When does complete healing of a slightly septic wound typically occur?
back: Healing is generally completed within 12 to 16 days after the initial injury.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [skin grows over it and healing gets completed in twelve to sixteen days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How does 'gravity shifting' affect the age estimation of a bruise?
back: A bruise may change its position and shape (e.g., a forehead blow causing a black eye) within 24 hours under the influence of gravity.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site... within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Why might bruises from repeated 'police battering' fail to show normal color changes?
back: Continuous trauma breaks tissues and interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action, causing the blood to darken rapidly to deep blue/black without the normal green/yellow sequence.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [repeated strikes... interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and prevents normal sequence of color change... rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue/black color.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What biochemical reaction is responsible for a bruise turning greenish?
back: Tissue enzymes begin converting hemoglobin into blood pigments like biliverdin approximately 4 to 5 days after injury.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the definitive differentiator between ante-mortem and post-mortem abrasions?
back: Ante-mortem abrasions exhibit a 'vital reaction' (inflammation or serum exudation), whereas post-mortem abrasions appear dry and parchment-like over time.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying gives a parchment appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the age of a bruise when it appears greenish in color?
back: 4 to 5 days after the injury.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Describe the biochemical mechanism for color changes in a bruise.
back: Tissue enzymes break down hemoglobin into various blood pigments over time.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Contrast the time required for scar formation in clean vs. septic wounds.
back:
• Clean wounds: 7 to 10 days.
• Septic wounds: 12 to 16 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [red linear scar formation in about seven to ten days... healing gets completed in twelve to sixteen days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: An abrasion shows a soft scab. What is its approximate age?
back: Approximately 2 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It is followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: When is the microscopic invasion of white blood cells first seen in a wound?
back: 4 to 6 hours after the injury (earliest sign of repair).
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically between four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the expected color sequence of effused serum in an aging abrasion?
back: Straw to yellow to brown.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown, depending upon the amount of blood.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How long does it take for a bruise to turn yellow and then disappear?
back:
• Yellow: 7 to 10 days.
• Disappears: About 2 weeks.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: An infected wound shows red granulation tissue in its bed. Estimate its age.
back: 5 to 6 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [followed by formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Why does a bruise darken specifically within the first two days?
back: Due to the deoxygenation of the effused blood.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: When does a clean, non-gaping wound show adherence of its edges?
back: 3 to 4 days after infliction.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [followed by adherence of edges in about three to four days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the timeline for the hardening and falling off of an abrasion scab?
back:
• Scab hardens: 3 to 4 days after formation.
• Scab falls off: 3 to 4 additional days after hardening.
• Total duration: Approximately 8–10 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It is followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism causes a bruise to turn greenish at 4–5 days?
back:
• Action: Tissue enzymes break down hemoglobin.
• Transformation: Hemoglobin is converted into specific blood pigments.
• Timeline: Starts becoming greenish in 4 to 5 days.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Differentiate the color of a recent bruise from one aged 7 to 10 days.
back:
• Recent: Purple (due to capillary blood).
• 7–10 Days: Yellowish (due to complete pigment breakdown).
• Disappearance: Usually 2 to 3 weeks.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [a recent bruise appears purple in color... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellowish and finally disappears in about two or three weeks.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: A septic wound shows red granulation tissue at the bed. Estimate the wound age.
back:
• Age: ~5 to 6 days old.
• Future Progression: Skin growth and healing completion typically takes 12 to 16 days total for such wounds.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [followed by formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days, skin grows over it and healing gets completed in twelve to sixteen days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the first microscopic cellular step visible in wound repair?
back:
• Action: Invasion of white blood cells (leukocytes) at the injury site.
• Timing: Becomes visible microscopically 4 to 6 hours after injury.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What are the defining physical criteria of a clean wound at 24–36 hours?
back:
• Surface: Covered by lymph and blood.
• Condition: Clot formation occurs within the first 24 to 36 hours.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping wound gets covered by lymph and blood, which clot in first twenty four to thirty six hours.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How is enzyme histochemistry applied to determine the age of very fresh wounds?
back:
• Method: Detecting increased enzyme reaction (e.g., alkaline phosphatase) at the periphery.
• Utility: Can be detected much earlier than standard histological changes like leukocyte infiltration.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Why might a bruise turn deep blue in hours rather than days?
back:
• Cause: Repeated strikes (e.g., police battering).
• Mechanism: Excessive trauma breaks tissues and interferes with normal enzymatic color progression, causing rapid darkening.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [repeated strikes to body part... breaks body tissues, interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and cause rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue color.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Describe the initial local loop of inflammation in a septic wound.
back:
• Response: Margins swell due to edema and vascular reaction.
• Timing: Occurs within the first 12 to 16 hours post-injury.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Slightly septic wound margins swell in first twelve to sixteen hours, followed by appearance of seropurulent discharge in about three to four days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the typical timeframe for scar formation in a clean wound?
back:
• Scar Type: Red linear scar.
• Completion: Process of healing is usually finished in 7 to 10 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Process of healing is completed with red linear scar formation in about seven to ten days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: At what time interval does a soft scab typically form on a healing abrasion?
back: - Approximately 2 days after the injury.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It is followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Why does a bruise typically change color to greenish around the fourth or fifth day?
back: - Tissue enzymes begin converting hemoglobin into blood pigments.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Compare the appearance of a 2-day-old bruise versus one that is 7-10 days old.
back:
- 2 days: Color darkens to deep purple.
- 7-10 days: Color fades to yellow.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: A non-gaping incised wound shows a red linear scar. What is the estimated age?
back: - Approximately 7 to 10 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Process of healing is completed with red linear scar formation in about seven to ten days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Which specific enzymes are used in histochemistry to determine the age of a burn?
back:
- Alkaline phosphatase
- Acid phosphatase
- Lucien amino-peptidase
- Non-specific esterase
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the timeframe for margin swelling in a slightly septic lacerated wound?
back: - Within the first 12 to 16 hours after injury.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Slightly septic wound margins swell in first twelve to sixteen hours]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What microscopic finding establishes a wound as being at least 4-6 hours old?
back: - The invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury (initial repair).
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
coreConcept: Modified Bruise Aging in Torture Cases
front: Q: How does color progression differ in bruises caused by repeated police battering?
back: - Repeated strikes interfere with enzymes, causing rapid darkening to deep blue/black within hours instead of days.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and accelerates color change from first two days to few hours causing rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue/black color.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Describe the final healing stage of an abrasion before the mark disappears.
back: - A hard scab forms (3-4 days post-injury), retracts (another 3-4 days), and falls away.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: When does red granulation tissue typically appear in a healing septic wound?
back: - Approximately 5 to 6 days after the injury.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [followed by formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the typical progression of color changes used to estimate the age of a bruise?
back:
* Recent: Purple
* 2 Days: Darkens
* 4-5 Days: Greenish
* 7-10 Days: Yellow
* 14-15 Days: Disappears
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Color changes depend upon ability of the tissue to absorb it... purple in color- darkens in two days... greenish in about four/five days... yellow within seven to ten days and finally disappears in about two weeks.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism causes the characteristic color changes in a maturing bruise?
back:
* Tissue enzymes break down hemoglobin into various blood pigments.
* Rate depends on tissue absorption ability and site depth.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Contrast the timeline for scar formation in clean versus slightly septic open wounds.
back:
* Clean wounds: Red linear scar forms in 7-10 days.
* Slightly septic wounds: Healing and epithelial growth take 12-16 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): Process of healing completed with red linear scar formation in about seven to ten days... [Septic] healing gets completed in twelve to sixteen days.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: An abrasion presents with a hard scab that is just beginning to retract. What is the estimated age?
back:
* Estimated Age: 8–10 days.
* 2 days (soft scab) + 3-4 days (hardening) + 3-4 days (retraction).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the earliest microscopic histological change used to confirm a wound is ante-mortem?
back:
* Invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.
* Occurs within 4 to 6 hours.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): It becomes visible microscopically in four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What are the diagnostic physical findings in a clean open wound within 24 to 36 hours?
back:
* Covered by lymph and blood.
* Clotting occurs within this specific timeframe.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): Clean and non-gaping wound gets covered by lymph and blood, which clot in first twenty four to thirty six hours.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How is the appearance of red-granulation tissue used to date a septic wound?
back:
* Indicates the wound is approximately 5 to 6 days old.
* Follows seropurulent discharge (3-4 days).
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): followed by formation of red-granulation tissue in the bed of the wound in about five to six days.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Why might a bruise change color faster than the standard 2-day darkening period?
back:
* Repeated strikes to the same part (police battering) cause rapid darkening within hours.
* It interferes with normal oxygenation/enzyme action.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): repeated strikes to body part... breaks body tissues, interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and color change from first two days to few hours causing rapid darkening.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What are the specific timelines for an abrasion's serum changes and initial scab formation?
back:
* Serum drying (straw to brown): First 24 hours.
* Soft scab formation: Approximately 2 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown... followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days.

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: At what point does a clean wound's epithelium typically adhere to the underlying surface?
back:
* Age: 3 to 4 days post-injury.
* Precedes the formation of a red scar.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): followed by adherence of epithelium in about three to four days. Process of healing completed with red linear scar formation in about seven to ten days.

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What are the primary gross physical signs indicating the ante-mortem nature of a wound?
back:
* Spouting of arterial blood.
* Presence of clotted blood.
* Retraction of wound edges.
* Signs of inflammation (swelling and redness).
citation: Page 82 (Book Page): [The form of vital reaction is initiation of the process of repair. It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells to the site of injury.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological mechanism behind the color changes in an ante-mortem bruise.
back:
* Tissue enzymes convert hemoglobin into pigments.
* Progression: Purple (fresh), Greenish (4-5 days), Yellow (7-10 days).
* Fading occurs due to fluid and pigment absorption.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish. Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption of fluid... yellow and finally disappears.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Contrast the appearance of ante-mortem versus post-mortem abrasions.
back:
* Ante-mortem: Shows vital reaction, congestion, and scab formation.
* Post-mortem: Looks parchment-like, yellowish, and dry; lacks inflammatory response or hemorrhage.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying presents different appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: In a charred body, which findings confirm the victim was alive during the fire?
back:
* Black sooty particles in the trachea and bronchi.
* Carbon monoxide (CO) saturation >70% in blood/bone-marrow.
* Ingested soot in the stomach.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood and other tissue like bone-marrow are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Which specific enzymes are used in histochemical determination of vital reactions in skin?
back:
* Alkaline phosphatase.
* Acid phosphatase.
* Leucine amino-peptidase.
* Non-specific esterases.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase... Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What microscopic criteria define a vital reaction in a healing wound?
back:
* Infiltration of leukocytes (WBCs) at the injury site.
* Becomes visible between 4 to 6 hours post-injury.
* Indicates active tissue response to trauma.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells to the site of injury.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: How is the 'Rule of Nine' applied during the forensic certification of burns?
back:
* It calculates the percentage of total body surface area (BSA) affected.
* Used to determine prognosis and lethality (fatal if >1/3 of BSA involved).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [During forensic certification, Medical Examiner takes advantage of the rule of nine to calculate the extent and percentage area involved bearing burns of the body surface.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Differentiate between a true ante-mortem bruise and post-mortem pseudo-bruising.
back:
* True Bruise: Blood is extravasated into interstices; shows swelling/inflammation.
* Pseudo-bruise: Blood is within vessels or displaced by gas pressure; lacks vital reaction.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [1. Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue... 2. Shows vital reaction (swelling and inflammation).]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Explain the physiological significance of 'retraction of edges' in a wound.
back:
* Occurs due to the elasticity of living skin and muscle tension.
* Is a classic sign that the injury occurred while tissues were viable.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Human body is composed of different types of tissues. They are soft and elastic like skin, fat, muscle... Bones of infants are relatively elastic.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What biochemical fact distinguishes ante-mortem burn vesicles from post-mortem blisters?
back:
* Ante-mortem vesicles contain plasma exudate rich in albumin.
* The base of an ante-mortem blister is raw and pink.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Pressure steam and liquids at high temperature cause blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin. Raw skin surface is pink.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the chronological color sequence used to determine the age of a bruise?
back:
- Fresh: Purple
- 2 Days: Darkens
- 4-5 Days: Greenish
- 7-10 Days: Yellowish
- 14-15 Days: Disappears
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Capillary blood is dark red in color and a recent bruise appears purple in color; darkens in two days... in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish. Fading of the bruise occurs... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the physiological mechanism behind the greenish discoloration in a 4-5 day old bruise?
back:
- Tissue enzymes act on the extravasated blood.
- Hemoglobin is biochemically converted into blood pigments (biliverdin/bilirubin).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Contrast the healing timelines of clean versus slightly septic open wounds.
back:
- Clean: Edges adhere in 3-4 days; red scar in 1 week.
- Septic: Seropurulent discharge in 3-4 days; granulation in 5-6 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping wound... adherence of edges in about three to four days. Process of healing is completed... in about a week. Slightly septic wound... seropurulent discharge in about three to four days... red-granulation tissue... in about five to six days]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: A victim presents with a bruise that is yellow. What is the estimated age?
back:
- Approximately 7 to 10 days old.
- This indicates the final stage of pigment absorption before total disappearance.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Which biochemical markers can be used to determine wound age via enzyme histochemistry?
back:
- Alkaline phosphatase
- Acid phosphatase
- Leucine amino-peptidase
- Non-specific esterase
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase... Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn... can be detected much earlier than histological changes.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What microscopic finding marks the initiation of wound repair at 4-6 hours?
back: - Invasion of white blood cells (leukocytes) at the site of injury.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically in four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How is the age of an abrasion determined based on scab characteristics?
back:
- Soft scab: 2 days
- Hard scab: 4-5 days
- Scab retraction: 7-8 days
- Scab falls off: 10-12 days
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Differentiate a fresh linear scar from an old one (over 10 days).
back:
- Fresh: Red color, completed in about one week.
- Old: Gradually changes from red to white or brown.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [red linear scar formation in about a week. Color of scar gradually changes from seven to ten days and eventually becomes white or brown.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What occurs during the metabolic loop of a slightly septic wound at 12-16 hours?
back: - Margins of the wound swell due to the onset of inflammation.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Slightly septic wound margins swell in first twelve to sixteen hours]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: When does a clean open wound typically achieve full edge adherence?
back: - In approximately 3 to 4 days.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping wound... followed by adherence of edges in about three to four days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What is the chronological sequence of color changes observed in a bruise?
back:
• Purple: Day 1
• Dark/Blue: Day 2
• Greenish: Days 4-5
• Yellowish: Days 7-10
• Disappearance: 2-3 weeks
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Age of bruise is estimated by the color of effused blood... recent bruise appears purple in color- it darkens in two days... becomes greenish in four/five days... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two to three weeks.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What physiological mechanism drives the color transitions in an aging bruise?
back:
• Tissue enzymes catalyze the breakdown of hemoglobin into various blood pigments.
• This process causes the visual shift from purple to green and yellow.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Contrast the healing milestones of clean versus slightly septic open wounds.
back:
• Clean: Clotting (24-36 hrs), Edge adherence (3-4 days), Linear scar (7-10 days).
• Septic: Swelling (12-16 hrs), Discharge (3-4 days), Granulation (5-6 days).
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Clean and non-gaping... clot in first twenty four to thirty six hours... adherence of edges in three to four days... red linear scar... seven to ten days. Slightly septic... swell in first twelve to sixteen hours... discharge in about three to four days... red-granulation tissue... five to six days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: A victim presents with a hard, retracting wound scab. Estimate the injury's age.
back:
• Estimated Age: 7 to 10 days.
• Progression: Scabs harden by days 3-4 and begin to retract or fall off by days 7-10.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: How is enzyme histochemistry utilized to determine the age of a wound?
back:
• Detects specific enzyme reactions (e.g., alkaline phosphatase) at the wound periphery.
• Identifies changes much earlier than standard macroscopic or microscopic histological observations.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Histo-chemistry at the periphery of the burnt skin indicates increased enzymes reaction... detected much earlier than histological changes.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What are the diagnostic criteria for identifying a fresh abrasion (Day 1)?
back:
• Presence of effused serum (yellowish/brownish fluid).
• Absence of scab formation (which requires at least 48 hours).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Compare the timeline for the first visible microscopic vs. macroscopic signs of repair.
back:
• Microscopic: 4 to 6 hours (invasion of white blood cells).
• Macroscopic (Naked Eye): Becomes visible significantly later (Days).
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [The form of vital reaction is initiation of the process of repair. It becomes visible microscopically in four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells to the site of injury. With naked eye, it becomes visible rather late.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Differentiate a standard aging bruise from a bruise caused by 'Police Battering'.
back:
• Standard: Progresses through colors over 10 days.
• Battering: Repeated strikes cause rapid darkening to deep blue within hours due to inhibited oxygenation.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [repeated strikes to body part... interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and color change from first two days to few hours causing rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue color.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: Describe the metabolic loop involving the disappearance of a 10-day-old bruise.
back:
• Hemoglobin is fully metabolized to yellow pigments.
• Local absorption by tissue clears the pigment within 2 to 3 weeks.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two to three weeks.]

category: Describe methods to determine age of wound
front: Q: What anatomical feature identifies a previously septic wound during the final scar stage?
back:
• The resulting scar is prominent and slightly raised above the surrounding skin surface.
• Clean wounds, by contrast, leave a simple linear scar.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Fresh scar in such a [septic] wound is more prominent and slightly raised over the surface of the skin.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What is the primary purpose of identifying a "vital reaction" in a wound?
back: To differentiate between an ante-mortem injury (inflicted during life) and a post-mortem injury by detecting physiological responses.
citation: Page 82 (Book Page): [Vital reaction is used to differentiate an ante-mortem wound from a post-mortem one.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: When does the microscopic vital reaction of "repair" typically become visible at an injury site?
back: Between four to six hours after the injury occurs.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [Ultimate form of vital reaction is initiation of the process of repair. It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours...]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Which specific cellular event characterizes the microscopic vital reaction of injury repair?
back: The invasion of white blood cells (leucocytes) at the site of the injury.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [...visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: How is an ante-mortem bruise distinguished from post-mortem pseudo-bruising/lividity?
back: By the presence of vital reactions, specifically tissue swelling and inflammation.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (anti-mortem)... vital reaction (swelling and inflammation).]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Which microscopic finding in skin confirms a burn occurred ante-mortem?
back: Infiltration of leucocytes, provided the burn is not full-thickness.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.6: Microscopy: Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration, provided the lesion is not of full thickness.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Which enzymes show increased histochemical reactions early in ante-mortem burns?
back: Alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, and non-specific esterase.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase... Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn...]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What macroscopic (naked eye) feature defines an ante-mortem burn?
back: A well-marked red line of inflammation (erythema), roughly 1/4 inch wide, bordering the lesion.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.6: Naked eye: Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What internal evidence confirms smoke inhalation occurred during life (ante-mortem)?
back: Black sooty particles in the trachea/bronchi and carbon monoxide blood saturation above 70%.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi... and the presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood... are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: How is throttling confirmed in a decomposed body where skin bruises are masked?
back: By identifying definitive ante-mortem fractures of the hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 155 (Book Page): [Decomposition may present difficulties... diagnosis of throttling will finally depend upon presence of fracture of thyroid cartilage or hyoid bone.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What biochemical characteristic of blood is associated with the vital process of asphyxia?
back: Blood remains in a fluid state due to the secretion of fibrinolysin by capillary endothelium.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Capillary endothelium under stress secretes fibrinolysin, which keeps the blood in fluid state.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What is the primary macroscopic difference between ante-mortem and post-mortem abrasions?
back:
* Ante-mortem: Shows vital reaction (hyperemia, swelling).
* Post-mortem: Lacks vital reaction; becomes dry and parchment-like over time.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Anle-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction... Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying presents a brown parchment-like appearance.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Contrast Bruise (AM) and Post-mortem Lividity (PM) regarding blood location and vessels.
back:
* Bruise: Blood is extravasated into surrounding tissue from broken vessels.
* PM Lividity: Blood remains within the vessels (stagnant).
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (anti-mortem): Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue... Post-mortem Lividity: Blood is within the vessels.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
coreConcept: Line of Redness in AM Burns
front: Q: Describe the characteristic macroscopic 'Line of Redness' in ante-mortem burns.
back:
* A well-marked reddening, roughly 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion.
* It indicates a vital response to thermal injury.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: A corpse has a neck abrasion; how is throttling confirmed as the cause of death?
back:
* Look for vital reactions like hyperemia or inflammatory edema around the abrasion.
* Check for internal evidence like bruising of neck muscles and fractures of laryngeal cartilages.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion especially when on Vital region like neck... Anle-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Which specific enzymes show increased reaction at the periphery of an ante-mortem burn?
back:
* Alkaline phosphatase and Acid phosphatase.
* Leucine amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase... Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: List the two respiratory indicators that confirm a victim was alive during a fire.
back:
* Presence of black sooty particles in the trachea/bronchi.
* Blood saturation of Carbon Monoxide exceeding 70%.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood... are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: How does the biochemical analysis of 'Blister' fluid differentiate AM from PM burns?
back:
* AM Blister: Contains plasma exudate rich in albumin.
* PM Blister: Contains only air or putrefactive gases.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Pressure steam and liquids at high temperature cause blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin... Postmortem artifact... skin splits... light in color and has a honeycomb appearance.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Differentiate between the base of an AM scald and a PM skin-slip artifact.
back:
* AM Scald: Base is red, raw, and inflamed (vital reaction).
* PM Skin-slip: Base is moist but lacks redness or vital reaction.
citation: Page 136 (Book Page): [The blisters... their base moist and showing no vital reaction are Postmortem blisters and skin-slip may wrongly be attributed to scalds.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: When does microscopic evidence of 'process of repair' (WBC infiltration) first appear in AM wounds?
back:
* Becomes visible 4 to 6 hours after injury.
* Manifested as the invasion of white blood cells at the injury site.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [The form of vital reaction is initiation of the process of repair. It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What does the 'marbling' appearance indicate in a decomposing dead body?
back:
* It is a post-mortem change due to bacterial breakdown of blood.
* Distinguishable from AM injury by its branching vascular pattern (sulfmethemoglobin).
citation: Page 136 (Book Page): [Bacteria... disrupt blood causing hemolysis... veins in these areas become prominent and visible due to accumulation of gases... and shows marbling stage.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What defines a "vital reaction" in forensic wound assessment?
back: The physiological response of living tissue to injury, used to differentiate ante-mortem wounds from post-mortem changes.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Which microscopic cell response identifies a wound as ante-mortem?
back: Leucocyte infiltration (white blood cell invasion) at the site of injury.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [It becomes visible microscopically after four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: How is a bruise distinguished from post-mortem hypostasis (pseudo-bruising)?
back: Bruises show broken vessels with vital reactions like swelling and inflammation; hypostasis is simple blood accumulation within intact vessels.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (Anti-mortem)... Shows vital reaction (swelling and inflammation).]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: In cases of burning, which finding confirms the victim was alive during the fire?
back: Presence of black sooty particles in the trachea or stomach, and >70% carbon monoxide in the blood.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood... are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: Which biochemical method detects ante-mortem wounding earlier than standard histology?
back: Enzyme histochemistry, specifically detecting increased alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, and non-specific esterases at wound margins.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What are the primary gross indicators of an ante-mortem burn?
back: 1. Line of redness (erythema) bordering the lesion. 2. Blisters containing albumin-rich plasma exudate.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.6: Naked eye... Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening... blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin.]

category: Describe different methods of determination of ante mortem/ post mortem nature (vital reaction) of a wound
front: Q: What is the significance of "active hemorrhage" in wound analysis?
