front: Q: Define the legal term "Hurt" as per the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Why is the maintenance of "Chain of Custody" mandatory when preparing a medico-legal report?
back: To ensure there is no chance of substitution, tampering, or adulteration of forensic samples between the place of examination and the laboratory for purposes of justice.
citation: Page 3 (Book Page): [Forensic Medical Examiner has to... adopt necessary precautions during collection, packing and dispatch of samples to forensic laboratory and maintains chain of custody of forensic samples.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Differentiate a "split laceration" over the scalp from an "incised wound" during physical examination.
back: Lacerations show irregular margins, ill-defined angles, bridging tissue tags, and crushed hair bulbs; incised wounds have cleanly severed tissues and hair bulbs without bridging.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags and hair in bearing area may get pushed into it with bulbs crushed.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Explain the mechanism behind "gravity shifting" of a bruise in a medico-legal examination.
back: Blood from broken vessels spreads along tissue lines of least resistance toward lower, dependent regions under the influence of gravity, occurring typically within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to lower region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Where is the standard site for recording inner core body temperature for a medico-legal report?
back: The rectum or sub-hepatic site (in sexual assaults). The thermometer bulb must be inserted four inches deep and recorded four times at 30-minute intervals.
citation: Page 132 (Book Page): [Usual site selected for this purpose is either rectum or sub-hepatic site... bulb of thermometer is placed about four inches deep into the rectum... Four readings, each at interval of half an hour should be taken.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the primary prerequisite before starting a medico-legal examination of an injured person?
back: Expressed written consent from the examinee is mandatory, except in life-threatening emergencies where implied consent applies for treatment.
citation: Page 6 (Book Page): [Expressed written consent of examinee, a prerequisite]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: How is the examinee's identity verified for the Medico-Legal Report (MLR)?
back: Identity is verified using the Computerized National Identity Card (CNIC) number and recording two permanent identification marks on the body.
citation: Page 109 (Book Page): [Record examinee’s personal identity verified from CNIC and also from his two identification marks]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What details must be recorded regarding worn clothes during a forensic trauma examination?
back:
* Type and condition (disturbed/torn)
* Evidence of weapon marks (knife cuts/bullet holes)
* Staining (blood, semen, mud, or grit)
citation: Page 106 (Book Page): [Examinee’s worn cloths type and condition weather disturbed, torn, bear knife-cut/bulle-hole or stained with blood/semen]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: In an MLR, how is 'Hurt' on the head or face classified if no bone is exposed?
back: It is classified as Shajjah-i-Khafifah under the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Khafifah: Hurt without exposing of bone.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What are the two distinct parts of a Medical Practitioner’s Testimony in court?
back:
1. Observed Facts: Site, size, shape, and margins of injuries.
2. Opinion: Causative weapon, age of injury, and gravity of hurt.
citation: Page 13 (Book Page): [First part comprises of observed fact... Second part is framed opinion or inference drawn by medical practitioner]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: How does a forensic examination differ from a routine clinical examination regarding liability?
back: The examiner must justify all recorded findings on oath in a Court of Law; clinical practice does not typically extend to judicial interpretation.
citation: Page 6 (Book Page): [Forensic Medical Examiner has to on oath present, interpret, authenticate and even justify all recorded findings]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What must an examiner look for to differentiate a split laceration from an incised wound?
back: Split lacerations have irregular margins, tissue bridging, and crushed hair bulbs, occurring where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Recognition of such a wound are... crushing of edges and at site of tearing hair bulbs of hair are crushed.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: When assessing the gravity of an injury in an MLR, what defines 'Jurh-i-Jaifah'?
back: Any injury that extends into the body cavity of the trunk (thorax or abdomen).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Why is 'low threshold of suspicion' critical when preparing an MLR?
back: Opposing parties may distort the history of allegation or substitute samples to obtain a favorable forensic certificate.
citation: Page 6 (Book Page): [Forensic Medical Examiner has to entertain low threshold of suspicion, while evaluating history of allegation]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What physical status parameters are essential to record in an MLR for a trauma victim?
back:
* Body temperature, BP, and Pulse
* Respiratory rate and character
* Pupillary reaction and skin pallor
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Cases of trauma needs recording of body temperature, blood pressure, pulse and respiratory rates... and pupil’s reaction to light]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the primary difference in objective between clinical practice and forensic medical examination?
back: Clinical practice focuses on treatment and patient benefit. Forensic examination focuses on the administration of justice, requiring a low threshold of suspicion and strict maintenance of the chain of custody.
citation: Page 3 (Book Page): [Comparing clinical practice with basic medicine practice indicates that they differ in examination objectives... Forensic Medical Examiner has to entertain low threshold of suspicion... and maintains chain of custody of forensic samples.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Explain the biochemical mechanism used to estimate the age of a bruise in a medico-legal report.
back: The color changes as tissue enzymes degrade hemoglobin into blood pigments. Purple/Blue: Recent-2 days; Greenish: 4-5 days; Yellowish: 7-10 days before disappearing.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, the color becomes yellow and finally disappears.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Distinguish between 'Shajjah' and 'Jurh' according to the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance classification.
back: Shajjah: Hurt specifically located on the head or face. Jurh: Hurt on any part of the body other than the head or face that bears a mark of a wound.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah: Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to Itlaf-i-Udw... Jurh: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face bearing mark of wound.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: A victim presents with multiple, parallel, superficial cuts on their non-dominant forearm. Diagnose the etiology.
back: Self-inflicted injuries (hesitation cuts). These are typically multiple, parallel, at accessible sites, and avoid sensitive or vital areas.
citation: Page 79 (Book Page): [Self-inflicted cuts are most common and they are multiple, arranged parallel to each other and on the accessible parts of the body such as scalp, arm, forearm and abdomen.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What mandatory step must be taken when collecting wet blood-stained clothing as forensic evidence?
back: Clothing must be air-dried on hangers to prevent decomposition, encircled with a permanent marker, and signed by the examiner before sealing.
citation: Page 107 (Book Page): [Wet stain is air dried and encircled with permanent marker before dispatch to the laboratory... cloths are air dried on hangers before they are handed over to police.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Name the two specific components of a Medical Practitioner’s Testimony in court.
back: 1. Observed Facts: Recorded physical findings (sites, sizes, shapes of wounds). 2. Framed Opinion: Inferences drawn (weapon type, age of injury, gravity).
citation: Page 10 (Book Page): [Medical Practitioner’s Testimony consists of two parts; First part comprises of observed fact... Second part is framed opinion or inference drawn by medical practitioner from above stated fact.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What internal autopsy finding confirms a victim was alive during a fire (Antemortem Burn)?
back: Presence of black sooty particles (carbon) in the trachea and bronchi, and a carboxy-hemoglobin level above 10% in the blood.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 10% carbon monoxide in blood... are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Compare the ligature marks in Hanging vs. Strangulation in a medico-legal report.
back: Hanging: Oblique, in-continuous (gap at knot), situated high in the neck. Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous, situated lower down (over or below the larynx).
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Oblique, Incomplete... High up in the neck. Strangulation: Horizontal, Complete... Middle of neck.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Describe the physiological response known as 'Vagal Inhibition' in neck compression.
back: Sudden cardiac arrest caused by stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve. It precipitates immediate death without classical signs of asphyxia.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Pressure on carotid sinus... Stimulates vagus nerve precipitating cardiac arrest... occurs almost instantaneous.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the mandatory legal prerequisite for the forensic examination of a living person?
back: Expressed written consent of the examinee. In the case of children, consent must be obtained from a parent or guardian.
citation: Page 3 (Book Page): [Expressed written consent of examinee, a prerequisite... age of majority i.e. eighteen years. In children under this age, consent should be obtained from guardian.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Define the three fundamental components of Ballistics.
back:
1. Interior Ballistics (within the barrel).
2. Exterior Ballistics (flight to target).
3. Wound-complex Ballistics (terminal effects on body).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Study of understanding of their cause-effect relationship of wounding with them is based upon a knowledge of special ballistics subject having three components: Interior ballistics, Exterior ballistics, Wound-complex ballistics.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism of Interior Ballistics.
back: Deals with the forces of propulsion of a projectile within the barrel bore, determined by barrel design and cartridge composition, ending at muzzle exit.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Interior ballistics deals with forces of propulsion of projectile (bullet/shot charge) dependent upon design of barrel and cartridge and remains limited within the bore of barrel till its exit from the muzzle end.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Contrast smooth-bore versus rifled firearm barrels.
back:
• Smooth bore: True cylinder or choked (e.g., shot-gun).
• Rifled: Spiraling grooves and lands (e.g., rifles/pistols) to induce spin.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Smooth bore may be a true cylinder or choked while rifled one has grooves and lands, which go spirally throughout the length of the barrel.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Clinical Scenario: A high-velocity bullet causes extensive tissue damage beyond the track diameter. Explain the mechanism.
back: Temporary cavitation occurs as high kinetic energy dissipates radially, causing tissues to expand and then collapse, leaving a permanent cavity larger than the bullet.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues... energy in the bullet is very high and it tends to dissipate in the surrounding tissues more effectively in radial fashion creating instant cavitation.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What chemical compounds constitute standard cartridge powder charges?
back:
• Black powder: Potassium nitrate, sulfur, and charcoal.
• Smokeless powder: Nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Powder charge... of two types; black consisting of potassium nitrate, sulfur and charcoal and smokeless consisting of nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: List the four essential parts of a Firearm Wound-Complex.
back:
1. Entry wound.
2. Trajectory with direction.
3. Bullet resting place.
4. Exit Wound.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex is name allocated to some-total resultant damage findings of fire-blast on target. It has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Define the velocity thresholds for Low vs. High velocity projectiles.
back:
• Low velocity: Less than 1200 feet per second.
• High velocity: Above 2000 feet per second.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Projectile velocity at the muzzle end is either low (less than 1200 feet per second) or high (above 2000 feet per second)]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Differentiate projectile behavior in soft tissue versus hollow fluid-filled organs.
back:
• Soft tissue: Radiates energy laterally (track/cavitation).
• Hollow fluid viscus: Contents displace explosively as secondary projectiles, leading to total disintegration.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [When a hollow viscus containing fluid is hit by a high velocity bullet, its contents get separated into particles, which get displaced explosively in all directions... and behave as secondary projectiles.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Explain the 'Chain of Events' stages triggered by the firing pin.
back:
1. Pin strikes primer.
2. Powder ignites liberating hot gases.
3. Chamber pressure rises (up to 20 tons in rifles).
4. Pressure forces projectile forward.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Strike of firing pin at the primer begins the chain... Powder charge gets ignited liberating gases at a very high temperature... Chamber pressure increased sharply... forces projectile to move forward through the bore.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Define 'Exterior Ballistics' and the primary forces influencing it.
back: The study of forces acting on a bullet in flight, primarily: projectile velocity (speed/direction), air resistance (negligible), and gravity.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Exterior ballistics deals with forces that act on bullet during its flight from the moment, it leaves the barrel to place of impact on the target... interaction between the forces originating from projectile motion, those present in the medium and force of gravity.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What are the three essential preliminary legal requirements before starting a medico-legal examination of an injured person?
back:
1. Examination by an authorized medical examiner. 
2. Written expressed consent of the examinee. 
3. Verification of personal identity.
citation: Page 6 (Book Page): [Only authorized medical examiner to undertake forensic medical examination; Expressed written consent of examinee, a prerequisite; Verification of examinee’s personal identity essential]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Describe the mechanical process and timing of 'gravity shifting' in the evaluation of a contusion.
back: Extravasated blood moves along tissue lines of least resistance toward dependent regions under the influence of gravity, typically occurring within the first 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to dependent region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: How is a 'split laceration' distinguished from an incised wound during a simulated forensic examination?
back: Split lacerations show irregular margins, ill-defined angles, and bridging tissue tags, whereas incised wounds have clean-cut edges and sharp angles.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags... It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: In a supervised environment, how must bloodstained or damaged clothing be documented and handled for a medico-legal report?
back: Identify damage (cuts/holes), encircle and sign them with a permanent marker, photograph the items, and air-dry on hangers before police dispatch.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [damaged portion encircled, signed with permanent marker, photographed and then cloths kept for air drying on hangers before they are handed over to police]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the standard protocol for collecting a stomach wash in a living victim of suspected acute poisoning?
back: Collect at least 500cc of the first wash using a chemically clean glass container, filling it only two-thirds to allow for gas collection.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Stomach wash is material of choice... Entire quantity or at least 500 cc is collected in a chemically clean glass container... Container should be filled to two thirds]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What specific color change indicates a bruise is approximately four to five days old?
back: The bruise becomes greenish due to the action of tissue enzymes converting hemoglobin into blood pigments.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Why is identifying a 'vital reaction' essential when preparing a medico-legal report for an injured person?
back: It differentiates ante-mortem injuries (showing swelling and inflammation) from post-mortem artifacts caused by rough handling of a corpse.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion... lacks vital reaction. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Differentiate the 'Opinion' section of a forensic medical certificate from a routine clinical diagnosis.
back: Forensic opinions must specifically state the weapon of causation (sharp/blunt), gravity (simple/dangerous), and age of injury (fresh/old).
citation: Page 10 (Book Page): [Second part is framed opinion... would include weapon of causation; sharp or blunt, gravity of injury: simple, serious or dangerous and age of injury; fresh or old.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism of the 'Hold-on effect' in domestic voltage electrical injuries.
back: Domestic voltage (220-240V) precipitates intense muscle spasms, which prevent the victim from releasing the live electrical conductor.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): [‘Hold-on effect’ at 220-240V (domestic) causes muscle spasm, responsible for non-release of live conductor.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Which preservative is contraindicated for viscera collected in suspected phosphorus or carbolic acid poisoning?
back: Rectified spirit is contraindicated; saturated sodium chloride solution must be used instead.
citation: Page 159 (Book Page): [Rectified spirit... is contraindicated in poisoning by phosphorus, acetic acid and carbolic acid.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What are the two primary methods used to verify the personal identity of an examinee in a medico-legal report?
back: 1. Recording the Computerized National Identity Card (CNIC) number. 2. Documenting two permanent identification marks on the body.
citation: Page 109 (Book Page): [Record examinee’s personal identity verified from CNIC and also from his two identification marks]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Under what specific clinical circumstance is "implied consent" applicable during a medico-legal examination?
back: Medical emergencies, such as a patient with profuse bleeding head injury, where immediate treatment is required to save life.
citation: Page 17 (Book Page): [Implied consent is applicable in cases of medical emergency. When a serious patient with profuse bleeding head injury comes to hospital emergency department... no time should be wasted in starting medical treatment.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Why must both positive and negative findings be documented in a formal forensic medical certificate?
back: To ensure transparency and provide a comprehensive document about the state of health for law enforcement and courts.
citation: Page 4 (Book Page): [Findings both positive as well as negative should be documented for information of requesting forum ie. administrative authority, law enforcement and law courts.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: A victim presents with a "moving abrasion" (graze); what forensic conclusion can be drawn from the epidermal findings?
back: The direction of the abrasive force can be determined by the piling up of the epidermis on the far end.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the specific role of potassium permanganate (1%) in the management of ingested alkaloids like opium?
back: It acts as a chemical antidote by oxidizing the poison within the stomach before it is absorbed.
citation: Page 169 (Book Page): [potassium permanganate, which is effective against all poisons capable of oxidation. It is used in strength of 1% solution... in cases of poisoning with barbiturates, cyanide, opium]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: In a suspected poisoning case, what are the volume and container requirements for collecting a stomach wash?
back: 1. Volume: Minimum 500 cc. 2. Container: 1000 cc chemically clean glass (filled 2/3). 3. No preservative.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Stomach wash is material of choice in all living cases of poisoning. Entire quantity or at least 500 cc is collected in a chemically clean glass container. Capacity... should not be less than 1000 cc. No preservative is used.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: How does the doctrine of "Res Ipsa Loquitur" affect the burden of proof in medical negligence litigation?
back: It creates an inference of negligence, shifting the burden of proof from the patient to the medical practitioner.
citation: Page 21 (Book Page): [Res Ipsa Loquitur... creates an inference that negligence has occurred and places responsibility on the medical practitioner to prove that he is not negligent.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: A patient presents with pinpoint pupils and shallow breathing; what is the primary diagnostic differential in toxicology?
back: Opiate (Narcotic) poisoning, requiring management with naloxone for respiratory reversal.
citation: Page 168 (Book Page): [Opiates produce vomiting, pinpoint pupils, slow and shallow breathing, unconsciousness ending into coma and death.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism by which a bruise (contusion) changes color over time.
back: Tissue enzymes break down hemoglobin into various blood pigments, progressively changing the color from purple to green to yellow.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Age of bruise is estimated by the color of effused blood... Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What mandatory environmental requirement must be met when examining a female victim for a medico-legal report?
back: The examination must be conducted in the presence of a female attendant, with the examinee performing her own undressing.
citation: Page 106 (Book Page): [In case of female victim, a female attendant should be present in the examination... undressing should be done unaided by the examinee herself]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What defines the primary difference in the 'threshold of suspicion' between forensic and clinical medical practice?
back:
- Forensic practice requires a low threshold of suspicion to detect distorted histories or substituted samples.
- Clinical practice assumes mutual interest in quick, accurate recovery without such interference.
citation: Page 3 (Book Page): [Forensic Medical Examiner has to entertain low threshold of suspicion, while evaluating history of allegation, adopt necessary precautions during collection, packing and dispatch of samples to forensic laboratory...]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What specific details regarding an examinee's clothing must be included in a standard medico-legal certificate?
back:
- Comprehensive description of worn clothes.
- Changes such as tears or stains.
- Special characteristics like trace evidence (e.g., hair) found in the fabric.
citation: Page 4 (Book Page): [besides physical and mental status of examinee; other details such as description of worm clothes along with any change in them torn or stained and other special characteristic such as trace evidence of hair in cloths are included in the medical certificate.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Explain the criteria for 'implied consent' in a forensic medical examination context.
back:
- Applicable only in medical emergencies (e.g., profuse bleeding from head injury).
- Immediate treatment is started without formal consent formalities to save the patient's life.
citation: Page 17 (Book Page): [Implied consent is applicable in cases of medical emergency. When a serious patient with profuse bleeding head injury comes to hospital emergency department, such circumstances imply that no time should be wasted in starting medical treatment. It should be started immediately condoning the formality of consent taking.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Describe the color progression used to estimate the age of a bruise (contusion) during examination.
back:
- Purple: Recent/fresh.
- Greenish: 4–5 days.
- Yellow: 7–10 days.
- Disappears: Approximately 2 weeks.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [recent bruise appears purple in color... in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish. Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption of blood; within seven to ten days, it tums yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What are the four essential parts of a firearm 'wound-complex' that a forensic report must describe?
back:
1. Entry wound (inverted margins).
2. Trajectory with direction (internal track).
3. Bullet resting place (if retained).
4. Exit wound (everted margins, if present).
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex is name allocated to some-total resultant damage findings of fire-blast on target. It has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Contrast the physical characteristics of 'hesitation cuts' in suicidal vs. homicidal cut-throat cases.
back:
- Suicidal: Multiple, superficial, parallel cuts near the main initiation point.
- Homicidal: Usually absent; the wound is typically single, bold, and deep.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): [Table 7.5: Contrasting features of suicidal and homicidal cut-throat... Hesitation cut: Suicidal (Near initiation point), Homicidal (Absent)... Number: Suicidal (Usually single), Homicidal (May be more than one).]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What are the three distinct stages of court evidence for a scientific witness in Pakistan?
back:
1. Examination-in-chief: Party producing the witness conducts it.
2. Cross-examination: Defending party tests credibility and accuracy.
3. Re-examination: Rectifies discrepancies from cross-examination.
citation: Page 9 (Book Page): [Stages of court evidence including medical practitioner’s evidence are three: Examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re examination.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Clinical Case: A victim presents with a 'spindle-shaped' wound with clean-cut margins and sharp angles. What is the etiology?
back:
- Incised wound.
- Caused by a sharp-edged weapon (e.g., knife or glass).
- The shape is determined by the weapon's movement and skin cleavage lines (Langer's lines).
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Wound is generally linear or spindle shaped, gaping in the center depending on cleavage lines of Langer. It shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the 'Viscera Trio' required for preservation during a forensic autopsy for suspected poisoning?
back:
1. Stomach and its contents (plus first 2 feet of small intestine).
2. Portions of liver, spleen, and one kidney.
3. Blood (100cc), bile (entire amount), and urine (entire amount).
citation: Page 160 (Book Page): [needs mentioning of trios of viscera/ fluid preserved separately... i. Stomach and first part of intestines... ii. Portion of liver, spleen and one kidney... iii. Blood, bile and urine]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Which microscopic and histochemical signs confirm a burn injury as 'ante-mortem' rather than post-mortem?
back:
- Microscopy: Leucocyte infiltration into the tissue.
- Histochemistry: Increased enzyme reaction (e.g., alkaline phosphatase) at the burn periphery.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Microscopy: Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration... Histo-chemistry at the periphery of the burn skin indicates increased enzymes reaction... detected much earlier than histological changes.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the primary difference in examination objectives between clinical practice and forensic practice regarding MLRs?
back: Clinical practice focuses on rapid treatment and labeling. Forensic practice requires a low threshold of suspicion, evaluating allegations, and maintaining a strict chain of custody.
citation: Page 3 (Book Page): [Forensic Medical Examiner has to entertain low threshold of suspicion, while evaluating history of allegation, adopt necessary precautions during collection, packing and dispatch of samples... and maintains chain of custody.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism of a "black eye" resulting from a blow to the forehead.
back: Effused blood from the forehead shifts along tissue lines of least resistance under the influence of gravity to the lax periorbital tissues.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to lower region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Contrast the characteristics of wound margins in lacerated versus incised wounds for forensic reporting.
back: Lacerated: Irregular margins with bridging tissue tags and crushed hair bulbs. Incised: Clean-cut, regular margins, sharp angles, and smooth walls with no bridging tissue.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins... walls that have bridging tissue tags... bulbs of hair... crushed.] Page 59 (Book Page): [Incised wound... shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: In an MLR for a thermal burn victim, which two parameters are essential for certifying the injury's gravity?
back: 1. Percentage of total body surface area involved (Rule of Nine). 2. Depth of the burn (superficial vs. full thickness).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Medico-legal certification important criteria for thermal burn are extent of body surface involved and depth of the burn.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the mandatory protocol for preserving a stomach wash for toxicological analysis in the living?
back: Collect at least 500cc in a 1000cc chemically clean glass container. Fill to two-thirds capacity to accommodate gases; use no preservative.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Stomach wash is material of choice in all living cases of poisoning. Entire quantity or at least 500 cc is collected in a chemically clean glass container... filled to two thirds of its capacity leaving upper one third of the space free for collection of gases... No preservative is used.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Define "Hurt" as specified under the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance for medico-legal reporting.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing/disabling/dismembering any body organ or part without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: How many permanent identity marks must be documented in an MLR, and what details are required?
back: Two permanent identity marks are required, documenting their color, size, and specific relationship to a fixed bony landmark.
citation: Page 109 (Book Page): [Record examinee’s personal identity verified from CNIC and also from his two identification marks... record full description about its color, size and relationship to fixed bony landmark.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Why might a "split laceration" be forensicially confused with an incised wound during examination?
back: On areas where skin is firmly supported by bone (scalp/chin), compression causes a split that resembles a clean cut. Bridging tissue tags confirm it is a laceration.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split laceration occurs on scalp... where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. Sudden compression... split them. It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the physiological significance of the "first hour" in blood collection for alcohol estimation in an MLR?
back: Ninety percent of alcohol is rapidly absorbed from the stomach and small intestine, reaching peak blood concentration within one hour.
citation: Page 178 (Book Page): [Ninety percent is rapidly absorbed both from stomach and small intestine in the first hour. Peak level in blood is reached in one hour.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Which microscopic feature distinguishes an ante-mortem abrasion from a post-mortem injury in a forensic report?
back: Vital reaction, indicated by the effusion of serum/blood leading to soft or hard scab formation and hyperemia.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction... followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
coreConcept: Legal Definitions of Hurt and Injury
front: Q: How does the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance distinguish between the terms 'Injury' and 'Hurt'?
back:
• Injury: Illegal harm caused to a person in body, mind, reputation, or property.
• Hurt: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or disabling an organ without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property. Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: In medicolegal reporting, what defines 'Shajjah' and where is it specifically located on the body?
back:
• Definition: Hurt on the head or face specifically.
• Exclusions: Does not include Itlaf-i-udw or Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw.
• Usage: Classified into six distinct subtypes based on tissue depth.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah: Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to thaf-i-Udw or itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Contrast the definitions of 'Jaifah' and 'Ghayr-jaifah' for reports regarding trunk injuries.
back:
• Jaifah: Hurt where the injury extends into a body cavity of the trunk.
• Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt on parts other than head/face that do not enter a body cavity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-Jaifah: Hurt not amounting to Jaifah.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Classify a head wound where the skin is broken exposing bone without causing a fracture.
back:
• Classification: Shajjah-i-Mudihah.
• Criteria: Exposing of the bone without its fracture.
• Significance: Higher legal penalty compared to Shajjah-i-Khafifah.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What is the purpose of leaving a 1% Potassium Permanganate solution in the stomach after lavage?
back:
• Action: Acts as a chemical antidote by oxidation.
• Target Poisons: Effective against alkaloids like morphine (opium), cyanide, and phosphorus.
• Quantity: Approximately 100-150 ml is left in the stomach.
citation: Page 169 (Book Page): [potassium permanganate, which is effective against all poisons capable of oxidation... 100-150 ml should be left in the stomach in cases of poisoning with barbiturates, cyanide, opium and phosphorus.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: What are the three primary clinical criteria for certifying a hurt as 'Itlaf-i-udw'?
back:
• Dismemberment of an organ or limb.
• Amputation of an organ or limb.
• Severance of any limb or organ of the body.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the badly.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Why is 'Chain of Custody' vital when examining a victim of alleged intoxication or poisoning?
back:
• Legal Necessity: Requires medical examiners to declare under oath that no tampering occurred.
• Purpose: Ensures the specimen analyzed in the lab is the same collected from the victim.
citation: Page 161 (Book Page): [All those who hold custody of these materials have to declare on oath in the court of law that no tampering of evidence took place while in their possession.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Distinguish a true ante-mortem bruise from post-mortem lividity during a medicolegal examination.
back:
• Bruise: Shows vital reaction (swelling/inflammation); blood is extravasated into tissues.
• Lividity: No vital reaction; blood remains within the vessels unless advanced decomposition occurs.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Table 1.3... Bruise (anti-mortem): Vital reaction (swelling and inflammation). Lividity: No vital reaction... Bruise: Blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: Describe the physiological mechanism behind sudden reflex cardiac arrest during manual strangulation.
back:
• Mechanism: Stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve.
• Result: Intense parasympathetic discharge leads to immediate circulatory failure and asystole.
• Significance: Death can occur without airway occlusion.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Reflex cardiac asystole takes place due to variations of tension within carotid sinuses... Sudden sympatho-adrenal or parasympathetic stimulation leads to circulatory failure.]

category: Examine and prepare medico-legal report of an injured person with different etiologies in a simulated/supervised environment
front: Q: In a medico-legal report, what color changes in a bruise indicate it is 4-5 days old?
back:
• Color: Greenish.
• Pathophysiology: Tissue enzymes convert hemoglobin into blood pigments like biliverdin.
• Importance: Crucial for determining the duration since the assault.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Define 'firearm weapons' and the categories included in this group.
back:
Dangerous weapons with multiple causative factors. The group includes:
* Revolver
* Rifle
* Shot-gun
* Bomb
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Firearms weapons as a group contain weapons like revolver, rifle, shot-gun and bomb.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Describe the 'chain of events' stages within the barrel during interior ballistics.
back:
1. Firing pin strikes primer.
2. Powder ignites, liberating gases.
3. Chamber pressure increases (4–20 tons).
4. Projectile moves forward.
5. Projectile acquires spin (if rifled).
6. Projectile exits barrel.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Chain of events takes place in six stages within the bore of barrel: Strike of firing pin... Powder charge gets ignited... Chamber pressure increased... forces projectile to move forward... Exit of projectile...]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Contrast the bore designs of smooth and rifled barrels.
back:
* Smooth bore: True cylinder or choked (e.g., shot-gun).
* Rifled bore: Contains spiral grooves and lands (e.g., rifle, pistol).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Smooth bore may be a true cylinder or choked while rifled one has grooves and lands, which go spirally throughout the length of the barrel.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: A victim presents with a stellate-shaped entry wound over a bony site. Explain the clinical mechanism.
back: This is 'blowback phenomenon.' In contact or high-velocity shots, hot gases enter the tissue, strike the bone, and return with force, distending and lacerating the skin.
citation: Page 72 (Book Page): [When there is hard bone as in scalp or cheek, it resists entry of gases, which return with extreme force; blowback phenomenon causing stellate or ragged wound with everted margin.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Contrast the chemical composition of black powder and smokeless powder.
back:
* Black: Potassium nitrate, sulfur, and charcoal.
* Smokeless: Nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [black consisting of potassium nitrate, sulfur and charcoal and smokeless consisting of nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What are the four essential components of a 'firearm wound-complex' for forensic certification?
back:
1. Entry wound
2. Trajectory (with direction)
3. Bullet resting place
4. Exit wound
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex is name allocated to some-total resultant damage findings... It has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Define the forces acting on a projectile during 'Exterior Ballistics'.
back:
Forces acting from barrel exit to target impact:
* Projectile motion (velocity: speed/direction)
* Air resistance (drag)
* Gravity (drawing bullet down)
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Exterior ballistics deals with forces that act on bullet during its flight from the moment, it leaves the barrel to place of impact on the target... interaction between the forces originating from projectile motion, those present in the medium and force of gravity.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Differentiate tissue tracks made by high-velocity versus low-velocity bullets.
back:
* Low-velocity: Perforates tissue with damage proportionate to bullet diameter.
* High-velocity: Produces temporary cavitation and extensive disintegration/disorganization of tissues adjacent to the track.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... additionally produces a temporary cavitation... larger than the diameter... disintegration and disorganization of large areas of the tissue immediately adjacent to the track.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Explain the pressure generation loop in interior ballistics.
back: One gram of ignited powder generates 200–900 ml of gas. This increases chamber pressure (4–6 tons for pistols, 20 tons for rifles), forcing the projectile forward.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [One-gram weight of powder generates 200 to 900 ml. of gas. Chamber pressure increased sharply from zero to four to six tons for a revolver... acts equally in all directions... forces projectile to move forward.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Define the velocity ranges for low and high velocity projectiles.
back:
* Low velocity: Less than 1200 feet per second.
* High velocity: Above 2000 feet per second.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Projectile velocity at the muzzle end is either low (less than 1200 feet per second) or high (above 2000 feet per second).]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: How are firearms classified based on the internal design of the barrel bore?
back:
1. Smooth bore: No internal rifling (e.g., shot-gun).
2. Rifled bore: Contains grooves and lands (e.g., rifle, pistol, revolver).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Barrel from point of view design... has a bore, smooth and rifled. Smooth bore may be a true cylinder or choked while rifled one has grooves and lands.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: Classify rifled weapons based on the muzzle velocity of their projectiles.
back:
1. Low velocity: Less than 1200 feet per second.
2. High velocity: Above 2000 feet per second.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Projectile velocity at the muzzle end is either low (less than 1200 feet per second) or high (above 2000 feet per second), depending upon with type of firearm.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: What are the two functional types of smooth-bore barrel designs?
back:
1. True cylinder: Uniform diameter.
2. Choked: Narrowed at the muzzle to control pellet dispersion.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Smooth bore may be a true cylinder or choked while rifled one has grooves and lands, which go spirally throughout the length of the barrel.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: A victim has multiple small pellets in a wound. Which firearm category was likely used?
back: Smooth-bore shot-gun. These utilize a "shot-charge" containing many small pellets rather than a single bullet.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Projectile is generally made of lead and is of two types; bullet that is single and shot-charge, which consists of many small pellets.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: How is the powder charge classified in firearm cartridges?
back:
1. Black powder: Consists of potassium nitrate, sulfur, and charcoal.
2. Smokeless powder: Consists of nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Powder charge... of two types; black consisting of potassium nitrate, sulfur and charcoal and smokeless consisting of nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: List the four weapons traditionally grouped together under the fire-arm/ballistics category.
back:
1. Revolver.
2. Rifle.
3. Shot-gun.
4. Bomb.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Firearms weapons as a group contain weapons like revolver, rifle, shot-gun and bomb.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: Classify firearms by barrel length and provide examples for each.
back:
1. Short-barreled: Revolvers and pistols.
2. Long-barreled: Rifles and shot-guns.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Barrel from point of view design is either long or short... Fig 7.1: Firearm design A. Twin-barreled smooth-bore shot-gun... B. Semi automatic rifled-barrel pistol.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: Compare chamber pressure between short-barreled and long-barreled rifled weapons.
back:
1. Revolver/Pistol: Low pressure (4 to 6 tons).
2. Rifle: High pressure (approximately 20 tons).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Chamber pressure increased sharply from zero to four to six tons for a revolver and pistol and about 20 tons for a rifle.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: Classify the projectile types based on the specific firearm used.
back:
1. Single bullet: Used in rifled firearms (pistols, rifles).
2. Shot-charge (pellets): Used in smooth-bore firearms (shot-guns).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Projectile is generally made of lead and is of two types; bullet that is single and shot-charge, which consists of many small pellets.]

category: Classify fire arm
front: Q: What defines a rifled bore firearm internally?
back: The presence of spiral grooves and lands inside the barrel that cause the projectile to spin on its axis.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [rifled one has grooves and lands, which go spirally throughout the length of the barrel... bullet besides acquiring acceleration is subjected to groove effect forcing the bullet to spin.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What is the medical definition of firearms as wounding implements?
back: Lethal weapons having multiple causative factors (e.g., revolver, rifle, shotgun, and bomb) capable of killing multiple people from a distance.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Firearms weapons as a group contain weapons like revolver, rifle, shot-gun and bomb... they are last of invented dangerous weapons having multiple causative factors.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Describe the "chain of events" stages occurring within a firearm barrel during firing.
back:
• Firing pin strikes primer.
• Powder ignites, liberating high-temp gases.
• Chamber pressure increases sharply (up to 20 tons).
• Pressure forces projectile forward with acceleration and spin.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Chain of events takes place in six stages within the bore of barrel... Strike of firing pin at the primer begins the chain... Powder charge gets ignited liberating gases... Chamber pressure increased sharply... Exit of projectile from the barrel brings the chamber pressure to zero.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Contrast smooth-bore and rifled-barrel firearm designs.
back:
• Smooth bore: True cylinder or choked barrel (e.g., shotgun).
• Rifled bore: Contains spiral grooves and lands to impart stabilizing spin (e.g., pistol, rifle).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Smooth bore may be a true cylinder or choked while rifled one has grooves and lands, which go spirally throughout the length of the barrel.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: A high-velocity bullet creates a cavity larger than its diameter. Explain the mechanism involved.
back:
• Produces temporary cavitation.
• High energy dissipates radially, pushing tissues laterally.
• Tissues recoil, leaving a permanent cavity larger than the projectile.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... energy in the bullet is very high and it tends to dissipate in the surrounding tissues... creating instant cavitation.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Differentiate between black powder and smokeless powder charges used in cartridges.
back:
• Black powder: Potassium nitrate, sulfur, and charcoal.
• Smokeless powder: Nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Powder charge varies... black consisting of potassium nitrate, sulfur and charcoal and smokeless consisting of nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: List the three essential components of the study of special ballistics.
back:
• Interior ballistics (within the barrel).
• Exterior ballistics (during flight).
• Wound-complex ballistics (target interaction/terminal).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Study of understanding of their cause-effect relationship... is based upon a knowledge of special ballistics subject having three components: Interior ballistics, Exterior ballistics, Wound-complex ballistics.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Which forces act on a bullet during the "Exterior Ballistics" phase of flight?
back:
• Propulsion forces (velocity and direction).
• Air resistance (negligible over short distances).
• Gravity (pulls bullet toward earth, creating a trajectory).
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Exterior ballistics deals with forces that act on bullet during its flight... interaction betweenn the forces originating from projectile motion, those present in the medium and force of gravity.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Differentiate the trajectory effects of a high-velocity bullet in soft tissue versus bone.
back:
• Soft tissue: Single uniform track proportionate to diameter.
• Hard bone: Bullet shatters target; bone fragments act as secondary projectiles creating multiple secondary tracks.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [When high velocity bullet strikes a bone... the bullet shatters its target more effectively... move and spread in various directions in the target as secondary projectiles... causing many secondary tracks.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Describe the mechanical purpose of rifling in firearms.
back: Imparts gyroscopic stability. By forcing the bullet to spin upon its axis, it prevents instability and tumbling once lateral barrel support ends.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page)-69: [In case of a rifle, bullet... is subjected to groove effect forcing the bullet to spin increasing its rotation upon its axis during forward motion... Sooner lateral support of barrel ends, forces of instability act on the bullet.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What are the four parts of a firearm "wound-complex" required for forensic certification?
back:
1. Entry wound.
2. Trajectory (with direction).
3. Projectile resting place.
4. Exit wound.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex is name allocated to some-total resultant damage findings... It has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Name the three standard components of a forensic ballistics study.
back:
1. Interior ballistics
2. Exterior ballistics
3. Wound-complex (target) ballistics
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Study of understanding of their cause-effect relationship of wounding with them is based upon a knowledge of special ballistics subject having three components: Interior ballistics, Exterior ballistics, Wound-complex ballistics]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of cavitation in high-velocity bullet wounds.
back: Energy dissipates radially, creating instant temporary cavitation larger than the bullet diameter, followed by tissue collapse into a permanent cavity.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Energy in the bullet is very high and it tends to dissipate in the surrounding tissues more effectively in radial fashion creating instant cavitation... leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Differentiate between low and high velocity projectile thresholds at the muzzle.
back: Low velocity is less than 1200 feet per second; high velocity is above 2000 feet per second.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Projectile velocity at the muzzle end is either low (less than 1200 feet per second) or high (above 2000 feet per second)]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: A high-velocity bullet strikes a long bone; describe the resulting internal wounding pattern.
back: The bone shatters, creating secondary projectiles that move in various directions, causing multiple secondary tracks.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page)-70: [When high velocity bullet strikes a bone... the bullet shatters its target... broken pieces of bones behave as secondary projectiles and spread in various directions causing many secondary tracks.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Identify the chemical composition of a standard firearm cartridge primer.
back: Barium, lead, and other metallic salts.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Primer is situated at the base having ability to fire and its composition is barium, lead and other metallic salts.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: List the four parts of a complete firearm wound-complex for forensic certification.
back:
- Entry wound
- Trajectory with direction
- Bullet resting place
- Exit wound
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex... has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Describe the first three stages in the chain of events within a firearm barrel.
back:
1. Firing pin strikes primer
2. Powder ignites liberating high-temperature gases
3. Gas production causes sharp rise in chamber pressure
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Chain of events takes place in six stages within the bore of barrel: Strike of firing pin at the primer... Powder charge gets ignited liberating gases... Chamber pressure increased sharply]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Contrast the tissue track shape of low-velocity versus high-velocity bullets in soft tissue.
back: Low-velocity creates a uniform course proportionate to bullet diameter; high-velocity causes massive disintegration and radial cavitation.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page)-70: [Low velocity bullet... causing damage proportionate to diameter of the bullet... characteristic of damage by high velocity bullet is disintegration and disorganization of large areas]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Explain how chamber pressure translates into projectile motion inside a rifled barrel.
back: Expanding gases exert equal pressure on the breech and projectile base; the projectile accelerates forward, acquiring spin from the grooves.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Chamber pressure acts equally in all directions... forces projectile to move forward through the bore accelerating... bullet besides acquiring acceleration is subjected to groove effect forcing the bullet to spin]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Differentiate between the two types of powder charges used in cartridges.
back: Black powder (potassium nitrate, sulfur, charcoal) and smokeless powder (nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Powder charge... thus of two types; black consisting of potassium nitrate, sulfur and charcoal and smokeless consisting of nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Which specific weapons are classified under the group of firearms?
back:
• Revolver
• Rifle
• Shot-gun
• Bomb
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Firearms weapons as a group contain weapons like revolver, rifle, shot-gun and bomb.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What is the forensic definition of ballistics?
back: The study of the cause-effect relationship of wounding produced by firearms or bombs.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Study of understanding of their cause-effect relationship of wounding with them is based upon a knowledge of special ballistics subject]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What are the three primary components of special ballistics?
back:
1. Interior ballistics
2. Exterior ballistics
3. Wound-complex (Terminal) ballistics
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [...having three components: Interior ballistics, Exterior ballistics, Wound-complex ballistics.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What is the scope of interior ballistics?
back: Propulsion forces of the projectile within the barrel bore until it exits the muzzle.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Interior ballistics deals with forces of propulsion of projectile (bullet/shot charge) dependent upon design of barrel and cartridge and remains limited within the bore of barrel till its exit from the muzzle end.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: How is exterior ballistics defined?
back: The study of forces acting on a bullet from muzzle exit to target impact.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Exterior ballistics deals with forces that act on bullet during its flight from the moment, it leaves the barrel to place of impact on the target.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What does terminal ballistics specifically investigate?
back: The effects of fire-blast contents on the human body target.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Terminal ballistics name is allocated to study of effects of fire-blast contents on the target on human body after coming out of the barrel of firearm.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Define the term 'Firearm wound-complex' in forensic practice.
back: The sum-total of resultant damage findings of a fire-blast on a target.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex is name allocated to some-total resultant damage findings of fire-blast on target.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Which two factors determine propulsion forces in interior ballistics?
back:
• Design of the barrel
• Design of the cartridge
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Interior ballistics deals with forces of propulsion of projectile (bullet/shot charge) dependent upon design of barrel and cartridge]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What three forces interact with a bullet during exterior flight?
back:
1. Projectile motion (velocity)
2. Medium resistance (air)
3. Gravity
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [During flight, there is interaction betweenn the forces originating from projectile motion, those present in the medium and force of gravity.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: How many stages comprise the interior ballistics 'chain of events'?
back: Six stages occurring within the barrel bore, ending at projectile exit.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Chain of events takes place in six stages within the bore of barrel... Exit of projectile from the barrel brings the chamber pressure to zero ending chain of events.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What are the three primary components of the special subject known as ballistics?
back:
1. Interior ballistics.
2. Exterior ballistics.
3. Wound-complex ballistics.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Study of understanding of their cause-effect relationship of wounding with them is based upon a knowledge of special ballistics subject having three components: Interior ballistics, Exterior ballistics, Wound-complex ballistics.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Describe the chain of events initiated by the firing pin striking the cartridge primer.
back:
1. Powder ignites, liberating high-temperature gases.
2. Chamber pressure increases sharply.
3. Pressure forces the projectile forward, accelerating it through the bore.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Strike of firing pin at the primer begins the chain. Powder charge gets ignited liberating gases at a very high temperature... Chamber pressure increased sharply... forces projectile to move forward through the bore accelerating continuously.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Distinguish between the wounding mechanisms of low-velocity and high-velocity bullets in soft tissue.
back:
1. Low-velocity: Pushes and rotates to produce a path proportionate to bullet diameter.
2. High-velocity: Dissipates energy radially to produce temporary cavitation and massive tissue disorganization.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Low velocity bullet... pushes and rotates to produce an indentation in soft and elastic tissues... High velocity bullet, on the other hand, additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: A victim presents with a stellate-shaped entry wound on the forehead. What ballistic mechanism explains this?
back: Blowback phenomenon: At contact range, gases enter tissue but are resisted by underlying bone, returning with force to lacerate skin in a ragged pattern.
citation: Page 72 (Book Page): [When there is hard bone as in scalp or cheek, it resists entry of gases, which return with extreme force; blowback phenomenon causing stellate or ragged wound with everted margin.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What are the two types of powder charges used in firearms and their chemical compositions?
back:
1. Black powder: Potassium nitrate, sulfur, and charcoal.
2. Smokeless powder: Nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Powder charge... thus of two types; black consisting of potassium nitrate, sulfur and charcoal and smokeless consisting of nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: List the four essential parts of a firearm wound-complex required for forensic certification.
back:
1. Entry wound.
2. Trajectory with direction.
3. Bullet resting place.
4. Exit wound.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex... has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: How does the "groove effect" in a rifled barrel influence ballistics?
back: It forces the bullet to spin on its axis during forward motion, providing rotational stability during its flight.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [In case of a rifle, bullet besides acquiring acceleration is subjected to groove effect forcing the bullet to spin increasing its rotation upon its axis during forward motion.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: How can a forensic examiner differentiate between a rifled weapon and a shotgun entry wound?
back:
1. Rifled: Typically a single circular hole.
2. Shotgun: Multiple pellet holes or central en-mass entry depending on distance.
citation: Page 74 (Book Page): [Main difference rifled wound has single hole whereas shotgun has many holes depending upon distance of fire.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What forces interact with a projectile during its flight in exterior ballistics?
back:
1. Projectile velocity (speed/direction).
2. Air resistance (negligible).
3. Gravity (draws bullet downward).
4. Gyroscopic forces (tip stability).
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [During flight, there is interaction betweenn the forces originating from projectile motion, those present in the medium and force of gravity.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Describe the characteristics of a "collar of abrasion" in a firearm entry wound.
back: It is a circular marginal ring caused by the bullet’s rubbing or screwing motion against the skin during vertical penetration.
citation: Page 71 (Book Page): [Abrasion ring is always marginal and appears circular when the strike is from vertical approach... Rubbing of screwing motion by bullet perpendicular to skin.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: How is a firearm weapon medically defined?
back: A dangerous weapon with multiple causative factors capable of lethal effects. It includes revolvers, rifles, shot-guns, and bombs.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Introduction to Fire-arm weapons is necessary, because of their more lethal effects and their ability to kill multiple people at a far distance. They are last of invented dangerous weapons having multiple causative factors. Firearms weapons as a group contain weapons like revolver, rifle, shot-gun and bomb.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What is the mechanism of action defined as interior ballistics?
back: The study of propulsion forces acting on a projectile within the barrel bore until its exit from the muzzle.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Interior ballistics deals with forces of propulsion of projectile (bullet/shot charge) dependent upon design of barrel and cartridge and remains limited within the bore of barrel till its exit from the muzzle end.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Contrast the anatomical design of smooth versus rifled firearm bores.
back: Smooth bores are true cylinders or choked. Rifled bores contain spiral grooves and lands to spin the bullet for stability.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Smooth bore may be a true cylinder or choked while rifled one has grooves and lands, which go spirally throughout the length of the barrel.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: A victim presents with multiple pellet wounds. What projectile type was used?
back: A shot-charge, which consists of many small pellets fired from a smooth-bore weapon like a shotgun.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Projectile is generally made of lead and is of two types; bullet that is single and shot-charge, which consists of many small pellets.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: What chemical components differentiate black powder from smokeless powder?
back: Black powder: Potassium nitrate, sulfur, and charcoal. Smokeless powder: Nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [powder charge... thus of two types; black consisting of potassium nitrate, sulfur and charcoal and smokeless consisting of nitro-cellulose and nitroglycerine.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: List the four essential components of a firearm wound-complex for forensic certification.
back: 1. Entry wound. 2. Trajectory and direction. 3. Projectile resting place. 4. Exit wound.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex is name allocated to some-total resultant damage findings of fire-blast on target. It has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Apply the principle of exterior ballistics to define bullet flight dynamics.
back: It involves interactions between velocity (speed/direction), gravity, and air resistance after the bullet leaves the muzzle.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Exterior ballistics deals with forces that act on bullet during its flight from the moment, it leaves the barrel to place of impact on the target. During flight, there is interaction betweenn the forces originating from projectile motion, those present in the medium and force of gravity.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
front: Q: Differentiate low velocity from high velocity muzzle speeds in ballistics.
back: Low velocity: Less than 1200 feet per second. High velocity: Above 2000 feet per second.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Projectile velocity at the muzzle end is either low (less than 1200 feet per second) or high (above 2000 feet per second), spending upon with type of firearm.]

category: Define fire arms and ballistics
